115824.e: Melvin Calvin and his team in Berkeley worked out the path of carbon in photosynthesis. That is why the cycle bears his name.
115824.m: Melvin Calvin was honoured for working out the carbon pathway of photosynthesis.

115825.q: Which isotope did Calvin and his colleagues use to trace the path of carbon in green algae?
115825.e: The algae were given radioactively labelled 14CO2. After short intervals, the labelled substances were separated and identified using paper chromatography.
115825.m: Radioactive carbon-14 made the Calvin cycle visible.

115826.q: Why is the Calvin cycle called “light-independent” even though it mainly takes place during the day?
a: It does not use light directly
It takes place outside the cell
115826.e: The Calvin cycle does not absorb any light itself. But it depends on ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, and several of its enzymes are only activated in light.
115826.m: The Calvin cycle needs light only indirectly, through the products of the light reactions.

115827.q: In which part of the chloroplast does the Calvin cycle take place?
115827.e: The enzymes of the Calvin cycle are dissolved in the stroma, the ground substance of the chloroplast. The light reactions, by contrast, take place on the thylakoid membranes.
115827.m: The Calvin cycle takes place in the stroma.

115828.q: Where in the plant cell are the photosystems of the light reactions located?
a: In the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplasts
115828.e: The photosystems are large protein complexes containing chlorophyll. They sit in the thylakoid membranes inside the chloroplasts.
115828.m: The light reactions take place on the thylakoid membranes.

115829.q: What is the light-driven splitting of water at photosystem II called?
115829.e: The oxidised P680 takes electrons from water via a metal cluster. In the process, water breaks down into oxygen, protons and electrons.
115829.m: The splitting of water in photosynthesis is called photolysis.

115831.q: What does the splitting of water at photosystem II provide?
115831.e: Photosystem II takes electrons from water, which then enter the electron transport chain. The protons help to make ATP, and the oxygen is released.
115831.m: Splitting water provides electrons, protons and oxygen.

115832.q: In which metabolic pathway do plants use CO2 to build sugar?
115832.e: In the Calvin cycle in the stroma of the chloroplasts, CO2 is built into sugar with the help of ATP and NADPH from the light reactions. The Krebs cycle, on the other hand, is part of cellular respiration.
115832.m: In the Calvin cycle, CO2 is built into sugar.

115833.q: Which two energy-rich substances do the light reactions provide for the Calvin cycle?
115833.e: In the light reactions, light energy is stored in ATP and NADPH. The Calvin cycle uses these substances to build sugar from CO2.
115833.m: The light reactions provide ATP and NADPH for the Calvin cycle.

115834.q: What does a herbicide that blocks electron transport in photosystem II do?
a: The plant can no longer carry out photosynthesis
The roots take up more water
115834.e: Without electron transport, neither ATP nor NADPH is made. The plant can no longer make sugar and dies. A well-known example of such a herbicide is diuron.
115834.m: Some herbicides stop photosynthesis at photosystem II.

115835.q: Why can very strong light harm a plant?
a: It damages parts of the photosynthetic machinery
It dissolves the chlorophyll in water
It makes the cell walls melt
It stops the roots taking up water
115835.e: In very strong light, reactive forms of oxygen are produced that damage proteins in photosystem II. The plant has to replace these parts constantly.
115835.m: Too much light can damage the photosynthetic machinery.

115836.q: What job does the enzyme Rubisco have in photosynthesis?
a: It binds CO2 from the air to a sugar molecule
It splits water and releases oxygen
It breaks down starch into sugar
115836.e: Rubisco is the key enzyme of the Calvin cycle. It fixes carbon dioxide, from which the plant then builds sugar.
115836.m: Rubisco fixes CO2 in the Calvin cycle.

115837.q: Which protein is considered the most abundant protein on Earth?
115837.e: Rubisco makes up a large part of the soluble proteins in leaves. Since it occurs in all green plants and algae, it is considered the most abundant protein of all.
115837.m: Rubisco is probably the most abundant protein on Earth.

115838.q: In which part of plant cells does Rubisco work?
115838.e: Rubisco is found in the stroma of the chloroplasts, where the Calvin cycle takes place. There, CO2 is processed into sugar.

115839.q: Which weakness of Rubisco leads to what is known as photorespiration?
a: It sometimes binds oxygen instead of CO2
It breaks down immediately in light
It needs nitrogen instead of CO2
115839.e: Rubisco can bind O2 as well as CO2. This produces a substance that the plant has to recycle at a cost in energy.
115839.m: Rubisco sometimes mixes up CO2 and oxygen.

115840.q: Roughly how fast does a single Rubisco molecule work?
a: Only a few reactions per second
About a thousand reactions per second
About a hundred thousand reactions per second
About a million reactions per second
115840.e: Rubisco is one of the slowest enzymes and converts only about 1 to 10 molecules per second. Plants make up for this with very large amounts of the enzyme.
115840.m: Rubisco is a very slow enzyme, so plants make a great deal of it.

115841.q: Which enzyme frees Rubisco from inhibiting sugar phosphates and so keeps it active?
115841.e: Sugar phosphates can block the active site. The ATP-dependent Rubisco activase removes them and makes the enzyme ready for work again.

115842.q: How do plants make up for Rubisco being a very slow enzyme?
a: They make very large amounts of it
They replace it with another enzyme at night
They do without the Calvin cycle
115842.e: A Rubisco molecule converts only a few CO2 per second. That is why a large part of the soluble protein in leaves is Rubisco.
115842.m: Plants make a lot of Rubisco because it works slowly.

115843.q: In plants, where is the gene for the large subunit of Rubisco stored?
115843.e: The gene rbcL lies in the circular DNA of the chloroplast, whereas the gene for the small subunit is in the nucleus. So both genomes have to work together.
115843.m: The large Rubisco subunit is encoded by the chloroplast itself.

115844.q: What drives ATP synthase in the membranes of mitochondria and chloroplasts?
a: A proton gradient across the membrane
115844.e: There are many more protons on one side of the membrane than on the other. When they flow back through ATP synthase, this provides the energy to make ATP.
115844.m: A proton gradient drives ATP synthase.

115845.q: What is the theory called which says that a proton gradient across a membrane drives the production of ATP?
115845.e: Peter Mitchell put forward the chemiosmotic theory in 1961 and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1978. It applies to mitochondria and chloroplasts.
115845.m: The chemiosmotic theory explains ATP production by a proton gradient.

115846.q: In which direction do protons flow through ATP synthase in the chloroplast?
a: From the thylakoid lumen into the stroma
From the stroma into the thylakoid lumen
From the cytoplasm into the stroma
From the stroma into the vacuole
115846.e: The proton concentration in the lumen is high. Following the gradient, the protons flow through ATP synthase into the stroma, where the ATP is also produced.
115846.m: In the chloroplast, protons flow from the lumen into the stroma.

115847.q: From which building blocks does ATP synthase make ATP?
115847.e: ATP synthase attaches another phosphate group to ADP. Exactly how this works was explained by Paul Boyer and John Walker, who received the Nobel Prize for it in 1997.
115847.m: ATP synthase joins ADP and phosphate to make ATP.

115848.q: In which membrane of the chloroplasts is ATP synthase located?
115848.e: ATP synthase sits in the thylakoid membrane, with its head part sticking out into the stroma. That is where the ATP for the Calvin cycle is made.
115848.m: In the chloroplast, ATP synthase sits in the thylakoid membrane.

115849.q: What is the production of ATP using light energy called?
115849.e: In photophosphorylation, light provides the proton gradient via the electron transport chain. In mitochondria, the corresponding process is called oxidative phosphorylation.
115849.m: Making ATP with light energy is called photophosphorylation.

115850.q: What happens if isolated thylakoids are moved from an acidic to an alkaline solution in the dark?
115850.e: It stays acidic inside and is alkaline outside. This proton gradient is enough for ATP synthase to make ATP even without light. André Jagendorf showed this in 1966.
115850.m: A proton gradient on its own is enough to make ATP.

115851.q: Why is ATP synthase called a molecular motor?
a: Part of it rotates when protons flow through
It moves the whole cell forwards
It burns fuel like a car engine
115851.e: The flow of protons sets a ring in the membrane and an axle attached to it spinning. This rotation changes the head part so that ATP is formed.
115851.m: ATP synthase is a molecular rotary motor.

115852.q: In which part of photosynthesis is NADPH produced?
115852.e: In the light reactions, light energy is used to make NADPH and ATP. Both are then used up in the Calvin cycle to build sugar.
115852.m: NADPH is produced in the light reactions.

115853.q: What job does NADPH do in the Calvin cycle?
115853.e: In the reduction phase, NADPH gives up electrons and reduces 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to a sugar. In doing so it becomes NADP+ again.
115853.m: NADPH is the reducing agent for making sugar.

115854.q: Where do the electrons stored in NADPH during photosynthesis ultimately come from?
115854.e: In the light reactions, water is split. Its electrons travel along an electron transport chain and finally end up in NADPH.
115854.m: The electrons in NADPH come from water.

115855.q: Apart from NADPH, which other energy-rich molecule is produced in the light reactions?
115855.e: The light reactions supply ATP as an energy carrier and NADPH as a reducing agent. Both drive the Calvin cycle.
115855.m: The light reactions supply ATP and NADPH.

115856.q: What happens to NADPH after it has given up electrons in the Calvin cycle?
a: It returns to the light reactions as NADP+
115856.e: NADP+ is a reusable carrier. In the light reactions it is loaded up again to make NADPH, so it shuttles between the two parts of photosynthesis.
115856.m: NADP+ and NADPH shuttle between the light reactions and the Calvin cycle.

115857.q: How does NADPH differ chemically from NADH?
115857.e: NADPH carries an extra phosphate group on the ribose part of the adenosine. This lets enzymes tell the two coenzymes apart.
115857.m: NADPH has one more phosphate group than NADH.

115858.q: On which side of the thylakoid membrane is NADPH produced?
115858.e: Ferredoxin and the enzyme that makes NADPH are on the stroma side. So NADPH is directly available to the Calvin cycle.
115858.m: NADPH is made where it is needed, on the stroma side.

115859.q: Where in the plant cell do the light reactions that produce NADPH take place?
a: On the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplasts
115859.e: Thylakoids are stacks of membranes in the chloroplast that contain chlorophyll and the electron transport chain. There, light is converted into chemical energy.
115859.m: The light reactions take place on the thylakoids.

115860.q: What are the stacks of thylakoids in the chloroplast, which look like piles of coins, called?
115860.e: A single stack is called a granum, several are called grana. Cristae, on the other hand, are the folds in mitochondria.

115861.q: What is the inner space of a thylakoid called?
115861.e: The thylakoid lumen is enclosed by the thylakoid membrane. In light, protons collect there.
115861.m: The inner space of a thylakoid is called the lumen.

115862.q: Where in the chloroplast are the thylakoids located?
115862.e: The thylakoids form a membrane system in the ground substance of the chloroplast, the stroma. The Calvin cycle also takes place in the stroma.
115862.m: Thylakoids lie in the stroma of the chloroplast.

115863.q: Which part of photosynthesis takes place on the thylakoid membranes?
115863.e: The thylakoid membranes contain chlorophyll, the photosystems and ATP synthase. There, light energy is used to make ATP and NADPH, which are needed in the stroma for the Calvin cycle.
115863.m: The light reactions take place on the thylakoids.

115864.q: What do seedlings that grow in the dark look like?
115864.e: Without light, the plastids make no chlorophyll and no finished thylakoid system. Only in light do green, working chloroplasts form within hours.
115864.m: Without light, seedlings form no finished thylakoids and stay pale.

115865.q: Which pigments are embedded in the thylakoid membrane?
115865.e: The thylakoid membrane contains chlorophyll a and b as well as carotenoids. These pigments capture light for photosynthesis.
115865.m: The leaf pigments sit in the thylakoid membranes.

115866.q: What job do the light-harvesting complexes in the thylakoid membrane have?
a: They capture light and pass the energy on
They pump water into the cell
115866.e: Light-harvesting complexes contain many chlorophyll and carotenoid molecules. They act like antennae and pass the light energy on to the reaction centres of the photosystems.
115866.m: Light-harvesting complexes are the antennae of photosynthesis.

115867.q: Which language does the word “thylakoid” come from, and what does it mean?
115867.e: The Greek word thylakos means sack or pouch. Thylakoids are flat, sac-like membrane vesicles.
115867.m: Thylakoids are named after their sac-like shape.

115868.q: What is called the stroma in the chloroplast?
a: The ground substance around the thylakoids
The inner space of the thylakoids
115868.e: The stroma is the gel-like fluid inside the inner envelope membrane. It contains the thylakoids, enzymes, DNA and ribosomes.
115868.m: The stroma is the ground substance of the chloroplast.

115869.q: Which metabolic pathway of photosynthesis takes place in the stroma?
115869.e: The enzymes for binding CO2 and making sugar are dissolved in the stroma. There, ATP and NADPH from the light reactions are used up.
115869.m: In the stroma, CO2 is turned into sugar in the Calvin cycle.

115870.q: During the light reactions of photosynthesis, where are protons pumped to from the stroma?
a: Into the inner space of the thylakoids
115870.e: In light, protons are pumped from the stroma into the thylakoid space. The resulting difference in concentration drives ATP production, and the stroma becomes slightly alkaline.
115870.m: In light, protons collect in the thylakoid space.

115871.q: What is found in the stroma that points to the bacterial origin of chloroplasts?
a: A nucleus with a nuclear envelope
115871.e: Chloroplasts have their own circular DNA and smaller 70S ribosomes, like bacteria. This supports the endosymbiotic theory.
115871.m: Their own DNA and 70S ribosomes in the stroma reveal their bacterial origin.

115872.q: Which storage substance is temporarily deposited as grains in the stroma during the day?
115872.e: If the plant makes more sugar than it can transport away, it stores it as starch grains in the stroma. At night this starch is broken down again.
115872.m: Surplus sugar is stored temporarily in the stroma as starch.

115873.q: How many envelope membranes surround a chloroplast of a land plant?
115873.e: The chloroplast is surrounded by an outer and an inner envelope membrane. The thylakoid membranes lie in addition inside.
115873.m: A chloroplast has a double membrane as its envelope.

115874.q: Which organelles of the plant cell have their own DNA, like the chloroplasts?
115874.e: Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own circular DNA and a double membrane. According to the endosymbiotic theory, both descend from bacteria that once lived freely.
115874.m: Chloroplasts and mitochondria have their own DNA.

115875.q: Apart from chlorophyll, which pigments are also found in chloroplasts?
115875.e: Carotenoids sit in the thylakoid membranes and in small fat droplets in the stroma. They help to collect light and protect against too much light. Anthocyanins, on the other hand, are in the vacuole.
115875.m: Besides chlorophyll, chloroplasts also contain carotenoids.

115876.q: In C4 plants, which molecule is the first product of CO2 fixation?
115876.e: In C4 plants, a compound with four carbon atoms, oxaloacetate, is formed first. That is where the name C4 comes from.
115876.m: The first fixation product of C4 plants is oxaloacetate.

115877.q: Which enzyme fixes CO2 in the mesophyll cells of C4 plants?
115877.e: PEP carboxylase joins phosphoenolpyruvate with a C1 unit to form oxaloacetate. It does not react with oxygen and works efficiently even when there is little CO2.
115877.m: C4 plants first fix CO2 with PEP carboxylase.

115878.q: Which weakness of the enzyme Rubisco do C4 plants get round?
a: In heat, Rubisco often binds oxygen instead of CO2
115878.e: Rubisco can bind oxygen as well as CO2, especially in heat and when CO2 is low. C4 plants concentrate CO2 around Rubisco and so reduce these losses.
115878.m: C4 plants protect Rubisco from binding oxygen.

115879.q: What is the typical leaf structure of C4 plants, with rings of cells around the vascular bundles, called?
115879.e: Mesophyll cells form a ring (German Kranz, wreath) around a layer of large bundle sheath cells. This arrangement allows the two fixation steps to be separated in space.
115879.m: C4 plants show a typical Kranz anatomy.

115880.q: In which cells of C4 plants does the Calvin cycle take place?
115880.e: The C4 acid is transported into the bundle sheath cells and decarboxylated there. The CO2 released is then fixed by Rubisco in the Calvin cycle.
115880.m: In C4 plants, Rubisco works in the bundle sheath cells.

115881.q: Which field crop common in Switzerland is a C4 plant?
115881.e: Maize comes from warmer parts of the Americas and uses the C4 pathway. Wheat, potatoes and rapeseed are C3 plants.
115881.m: Maize is the best-known C4 plant on Swiss fields.

115882.q: Which important tropical sugar crop is a C4 plant?
115882.e: Sugar cane is a grass and carries out highly productive C4 photosynthesis. Sugar beet, which is grown in Switzerland, is a C3 plant.
115882.m: Sugar cane is a particularly productive C4 plant.

115883.q: Why do C4 plants have an advantage in heat and drought?
a: They carry out no light reactions
115883.e: Thanks to pre-fixation, CO2 is strongly concentrated in the bundle sheath cells. This keeps photosynthesis efficient even when the stomata are partly closed.
115883.m: C4 plants concentrate CO2 and therefore work efficiently in heat.

115884.q: What does the abbreviation CAM stand for in plants?
115884.e: This metabolism was discovered in the stonecrop family (Crassulaceae), which gave it its name.

115885.q: When do CAM plants mainly open their stomata?
115885.e: At night it is cooler and more humid, so little water evaporates during gas exchange. During the day the stomata stay closed.
115885.m: CAM plants take in CO2 at night.

115886.q: In which form do CAM plants store the CO2 they take in at night?
a: As malic acid in the vacuole
As gas in the intercellular spaces
115886.e: The CO2 is bound to a C3 molecule and collected as malate (malic acid) in the large vacuole. That is why the leaves are noticeably more acidic in the morning.
115886.m: CAM plants store CO2 at night as malic acid.

115887.q: Which crop plant is a CAM plant?
115887.e: The pineapple is a bromeliad from dry regions and uses CAM metabolism. Maize is a C4 plant, wheat and sunflowers are C3 plants.
115887.m: The pineapple carries out CAM photosynthesis.

115888.q: What is the basic difference between CAM plants and C4 plants?
a: Separation in time instead of in space
Separation in space instead of in time
115888.e: C4 plants split pre-fixation and the Calvin cycle between different cells. CAM plants do both in the same cell, but at different times of day.
115888.m: CAM plants separate the steps in time, C4 plants in space.

115889.q: Which plant native to the Swiss Alps belongs to the stonecrop family, after which CAM is named?
115889.e: The houseleek (Sempervivum) grows on rocks and walls and stores water in its thick leaves. Like stonecrop, it belongs to the Crassulaceae.
115889.m: The houseleek is an Alpine member of the stonecrop family.

115890.q: What is the most important advantage of CAM metabolism?
a: It saves a great deal of water
It makes the plant grow faster
115890.e: Because the stomata stay closed during the day, CAM plants lose much less water per CO2 bound. In return, they usually grow slowly.
115890.m: CAM is an adaptation to water shortage.

115891.q: Where does the Calvin cycle of a CAM plant get its CO2 from during the day?
a: From the soil via the roots
115891.e: During the day, the acid stored at night is taken from the vacuole and decarboxylated. With the stomata closed, the released CO2 goes into the Calvin cycle.
115891.m: During the day, CAM plants release the stored CO2 again.

a: Rubisco binds O2 instead of CO2
The plant only respires at night
115892.e: The oxygenase reaction of Rubisco produces a molecule that the plant has to recycle at great effort. This recovery pathway is called photorespiration.
115892.m: Photorespiration begins when Rubisco binds oxygen instead of CO2.

115893.q: Which enzyme binds CO2 in photosynthesis and is considered the most abundant protein on Earth?
115893.e: In the Calvin cycle, Rubisco builds CO2 into organic molecules. Because it works slowly, plants make huge amounts of it. But it can also bind O2, which leads to photorespiration.
115893.m: Rubisco binds CO2 and is the most abundant protein on Earth.

115894.q: In which three organelles does photorespiration take place?
115894.e: Glycolate moves from the chloroplast to the peroxisome and, as glycine, on into the mitochondrion. The carbon returns to the chloroplast via the peroxisome.
115894.m: Chloroplast, peroxisome and mitochondrion are involved in photorespiration.

115895.q: Which gas is released in the mitochondria during photorespiration and lost to the plant?
115895.e: When two glycine molecules are converted, one carbon atom is given off as CO2. Carbon that has already been fixed is lost again in this way.
115895.m: Photorespiration releases CO2 that had already been fixed.

115896.q: Which crop is a C4 plant and therefore hardly suffers from photorespiration?
115896.e: C4 plants such as maize concentrate CO2 in special cells around Rubisco. As a result, the enzyme hardly binds any oxygen and photorespiration stays low. Wheat, potatoes and rice are C3 plants.
115896.m: C4 plants such as maize largely avoid photorespiration.

115897.q: Under which conditions is photorespiration particularly strong in C3 plants?
115897.e: In drought the stomata close, the CO2 level in the leaf falls and O2 builds up. High temperatures increase the oxygenase reaction even more.

115898.q: Why does photorespiration increase as the temperature rises?
a: CO2 dissolves less well than O2 in warmth
115898.e: As temperature rises, the solubility of CO2 falls more than that of O2. In addition, Rubisco prefers CO2 over O2 less clearly when it is warm.
115898.m: Warmth shifts the balance at Rubisco in favour of oxygen.

115899.q: Which toxic by-product forms in the peroxisome during photorespiration and is broken down by catalase?
115899.e: In the peroxisome, glycolate is oxidised, producing hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). The enzyme catalase quickly splits it into water and oxygen.
115899.m: Catalase breaks down toxic hydrogen peroxide.

115900.q: Why can red algae carry out photosynthesis even in deeper water?
a: Their accessory pigments also use green light
They need no light at all
They take up sugar from the water
They use heat from the seabed
115900.e: Red light is quickly absorbed in water, while green and blue light penetrate deeper. Red algae have accessory pigments, the phycobilins, that absorb exactly this light well.
115900.m: Red algae use green light too, thanks to accessory pigments.

115901.q: Why do most leaves look green?
a: Green light is absorbed only a little
Green light is used the most
115901.e: Green light is mostly reflected or let through. This light reaches our eyes, which is why leaves look green.
115901.m: Leaves look green because they hardly use green light.

115902.q: What is a graph called that shows the rate of photosynthesis depending on the wavelength?
115902.e: The absorption spectrum shows how strongly a pigment absorbs light. The action spectrum shows how strongly photosynthesis actually takes place at each wavelength.
115902.m: The action spectrum shows the rate of photosynthesis for each wavelength.

115903.q: Who showed in 1882, using bacteria that gathered around illuminated algal filaments, which light drives photosynthesis?
115903.e: Engelmann lit a filamentous alga with light spread out by a prism. Oxygen-loving bacteria gathered where blue and red light fell.
115903.m: Engelmann's bacteria experiment showed the first action spectrum.

115904.q: Which yellow to orange pigments extend the absorption spectrum and become visible in autumn?
115904.e: Carotenoids absorb blue and blue-green light and pass the energy on to chlorophyll. When the chlorophyll is broken down in autumn, they show through.
115904.m: Carotenoids are yellow-orange helper pigments of photosynthesis.

115905.q: Which wavelength range counts as photosynthetically active radiation?
115905.e: Plants use almost only visible light from about 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red). UV and infrared radiation contribute hardly anything to photosynthesis.
115905.m: Visible light from about 400 to 700 nm is photosynthetically active.

115906.q: Which central atom sits in the porphyrin ring of chlorophyll?
115906.e: Chlorophyll is built in a similar way to haem, the red pigment in blood. In haem, however, iron sits at the centre.
115906.m: A magnesium atom sits at the centre of chlorophyll.

115907.q: How many photosystems work together in the light reactions of plants?
115907.e: Photosystem II and photosystem I work one after the other. Robert Emerson showed that there are two: two wavelengths together had a stronger effect than the sum of each on its own.
115907.m: Plants use two photosystems that work together.

115908.q: Which chlorophyll is found in the reaction centres of all plants?
115908.e: Chlorophyll a forms the reaction centres of both photosystems. Chlorophyll b acts as a helper pigment in the antennae.
115908.m: Chlorophyll a is the central pigment of photosynthesis.

115909.q: What is meant by the nocebo effect?
a: A medicine works faster than expected
An illness heals for no reason
A doctor prescribes the wrong medicine
115909.e: If you expect something to harm you, you can really get symptoms such as a headache or nausea. The trigger is the expectation, not an active substance.
115909.m: In the nocebo effect, negative expectations cause symptoms.

115910.q: What does the Latin word “nocebo” mean?
115910.e: “Nocebo” comes from the Latin verb nocere, to harm. The form nocebo is the future tense and means “I will harm”.

115911.q: What is the counterpart of the nocebo effect called, in which positive expectations help?
115911.e: In the placebo effect, people feel better because they expect an effect. In the nocebo effect it is the other way round.
115911.m: The placebo and nocebo effects are two sides of expectation.

115912.q: How can doctors reduce nocebo effects?
a: Inform calmly and in a balanced way about risks
Describe side effects as dramatically as possible
Not talk to patients at all
115912.e: Explaining calmly how rare side effects are and what works well reduces fear. Important risks are still mentioned honestly.
115912.m: Calm and honest information can reduce nocebo effects.

115913.q: Why are people in the dummy pill group also asked about side effects in drug trials?
a: To separate real side effects from the effects of expectation
115913.e: People taking a sugar pill also often report side effects. Only by comparing can you see which symptoms really come from the active substance.
115913.m: Only comparing with the dummy pill group shows real side effects.

115914.q: What can make a nocebo effect stronger?
115914.e: If you read a long list of possible side effects and are afraid of them, you are more likely to feel such symptoms. Fear strengthens the negative expectation.
115914.m: Fear and worry can strengthen the nocebo effect.

115915.q: People next to a mobile phone mast complain of headaches, even when it has been switched off without them knowing. What best explains this?
115915.e: In such blind tests, the symptoms appeared regardless of whether the mast was really transmitting. What mattered was whether the people expected to be affected.
115915.m: Symptoms without a real cause can come from expectation.

115916.q: Is it true that symptoms from the nocebo effect are only put on?
a: Yes, they are always made up
Yes, they only happen in dreams
115916.e: Expectation affects the brain and body, for example through stress hormones. The symptoms are therefore real, even if no harmful substance is involved.
115916.m: Nocebo symptoms are real, not imagined.

115917.q: What does the ten per cent myth claim?
a: We only use 10 per cent of our brain
We sleep 10 per cent of our life
We forget 10 per cent of every day
115917.e: The myth says that 90 per cent of the brain lies unused. This idea is widespread, but wrong.
115917.m: The ten per cent myth claims we hardly use our brain.

115918.q: What does brain research say about the ten per cent myth?
a: Practically all areas of the brain are used
Only geniuses use more than 10 per cent
115918.e: Studies show that all brain regions have tasks. Over the course of the day, practically all areas are active, though not all at the same time.

115919.q: Which method can show which brain areas are active at the moment?
115919.e: Functional MRI measures where more oxygen-rich blood flows in the brain. This shows active regions, and no large unused part appears.
115919.m: Functional MRI shows which parts of the brain are working.

115920.q: Roughly how much of the body's energy does the brain use, even though it makes up only about 2 per cent of body weight?
115920.e: The brain is a very energy-hungry organ and uses about a fifth of the energy. An organ that was 90 per cent unused would be far too costly for this.
115920.m: The brain uses about a fifth of our energy.

115921.q: Which observation from medicine speaks against the ten per cent myth?
a: Even small brain injuries can have serious effects
People can live without a brain
115921.e: After a stroke in a small area, speech or movement, for example, can be affected. If 90 per cent of the area were unused, many injuries would have no effect.
115921.m: Because every brain area has a task, even small injuries cause harm.

115922.q: Why is the ten per cent myth so persistent?
a: It was proven in the laboratory
It is in every biology book
115922.e: The idea that you could awaken a huge unused potential is tempting. That is why it is often used in adverts, films and self-help books.
115922.m: The myth is popular because it promises secret superpowers.

115923.q: What would happen if all nerve cells fired at maximum at the same time?
a: You would no longer need sleep
115923.e: Healthy brain activity is finely tuned; not all cells are active at once. In an epileptic seizure, a great many nerve cells fire together out of control.
115923.m: A healthy brain works in a coordinated way, not with all cells at once.

115924.q: What is known about the origin of the ten per cent claim?
a: It is unclear; there is no study behind it
It comes from an experiment in 1990
It was announced by the WHO
It comes from a measurement on monkeys
115924.e: It is not clear who first spread the myth. In any case, there is no scientific study that supports it.
115924.m: There is no scientific evidence for the ten per cent myth.

115925.q: What are deliberately spread false reports often called?
115925.e: “Fake” means forged or false. Fake news is made-up or distorted news that looks like real reports.

115926.q: In German, which animal stands for a false report in a newspaper?
115926.e: In German, a made-up newspaper report is called a “Zeitungsente” (newspaper duck) or simply an “Ente”. Where the expression comes from is not completely clear.
115926.m: In German, a false newspaper report is called a duck.

a: A false report passed on as a warning
115927.e: A hoax is, for example, a supposed warning about a virus that you are told to send to all your contacts. This makes the false report spread further and further.
115927.m: A hoax is a false report that asks to be passed on.

115928.q: What did a large MIT study from 2018 find out about reports on Twitter?
a: False things spread faster than true things
115928.e: The researchers studied data from over ten years. False reports reached more people, and faster, probably because they seem more surprising.
115928.m: False reports often spread faster online than the truth.

115929.q: What makes satire different from a false report?
a: Satire wants to exaggerate in an obvious way
Satire only appears on the radio
115929.e: Satire exaggerates on purpose to make people laugh or think, and does not want to deceive. But if it is misunderstood, it can still be passed on as a false report.
115929.m: Satire exaggerates on purpose and does not want to deceive.

115930.q: What is a sensational headline mainly meant to get you to click on called?
115930.e: “Clickbait” is bait to make you click. Such headlines often promise more than the article delivers.
115930.m: Clickbait lures you to click with exaggerated headlines.

115931.q: What are automatically controlled accounts that spread posts on social networks in huge numbers called?
115931.e: Social bots are programs that seem like real users. They can share false reports very often in a short time.
115931.m: Social bots are programs that post like people.

115932.q: Which famous BBC April Fool's joke from 1957 was set in Ticino?
115932.e: The programme “Panorama” showed women supposedly picking spaghetti from trees. Many viewers believed it and asked how to plant spaghetti trees.
115932.m: Even serious broadcasters can fool many people with an April Fool's joke.

a: Mainly noticing what supports your own opinion
115933.e: People often look for, remember and interpret information so that it fits their own opinion. Contradicting evidence tends to be overlooked.
115933.m: With confirmation bias, we prefer what fits our own opinion.

115935.q: A football fan mainly remembers refereeing mistakes against his team. Which thinking error does this show?
115935.e: The fan believes the referee is against his team and remembers matching scenes especially well. Decisions in favour of his team stand out less to him.
115935.m: We remember especially well what fits our opinion.

115936.q: What is it called when algorithms show a person almost only content that fits their views?
115936.e: Platforms often show what you have liked before. So you see other opinions less and less, which strengthens confirmation bias.
115936.m: In a filter bubble, you see almost only what confirms your views.

115937.q: What is a group called in which everyone reinforces each other's opinions and opposing voices are missing?
115937.e: In an echo chamber, your own opinion bounces back like an echo. This makes it seem more certain than it perhaps is.
115937.m: In an echo chamber, you only hear the echo of your own opinion.

115938.q: In Peter Wason's number puzzle “2, 4, 6”, most people only tested sequences that confirmed their guess. Which thinking error did this show?
115938.e: The rule was simply “numbers going up”. Anyone who only checked confirming examples such as 8, 10, 12 hardly found the real rule, because they never tried to disprove it.
115938.m: If you only look for confirmation, you often do not find the truth.

115939.q: What helps most against confirmation bias?
115939.e: If you deliberately look for evidence against your own opinion, you test it more honestly. That is also how science works.
115939.m: Looking for counter-evidence helps against confirmation bias.

115940.q: Many people believe that A&E departments are busier at full moon. Why does this belief persist, even though studies find no link?
a: Hectic full-moon nights are remembered better
There are more doctors at full moon
It is always hot at full moon
115940.e: A hectic full-moon night fits the expectation and is remembered well. Quiet full-moon nights and hectic nights without a full moon are easily forgotten.

115941.q: What is typical of a conspiracy theory?
a: A secret plan by a group is supposed to explain everything
It is based on many measurements
115941.e: Conspiracy theories explain events by saying that a powerful group secretly controls everything. Evidence for this is usually missing.
115941.m: Conspiracy theories see a secret plan behind events.

115942.q: How do believers in conspiracy theories often react to counter-evidence?
a: They see it as part of the conspiracy
They change their minds at once
They ask for more evidence and check it
115942.e: Counter-evidence is then seen as a forgery by the conspirators. This means the theory can no longer be disproved at all.
115942.m: Conspiracy theories make themselves immune to being disproved.

115943.q: Which basic assumption is typical of conspiracy stories?
115943.e: In conspiracy stories, everything is planned and connected. Chance or simple mistakes are rejected as an explanation.
115943.m: Conspiracy stories do not accept chance.

115944.q: Which piece of evidence shows that people really were on the moon?
a: Laser reflectors left there are still targeted today
The moon can be seen from Earth
There is moon rock in every garden
115944.e: The Apollo astronauts set up mirrors on the moon. Observatories still send laser beams there today and so measure the distance to the moon.
115944.m: Mirrors from the Apollo missions on the moon prove the landings.

115945.q: What are the white trails behind aeroplanes mainly made of?
115945.e: The exhaust gases of the engines contain water vapour, which freezes into ice crystals in the cold air. Whether a trail stays for a long time depends on the humidity.

115946.q: Why do some people believe in conspiracy theories especially in uncertain times?
115946.e: In crises, many people feel helpless. A simple story with clear culprits seems to give support and a feeling of control.
115946.m: Simple explanations are especially tempting in crises.

115947.q: Why are huge secret conspiracies with thousands of people involved unlikely?
a: With many people in the know, someone is sure to give something away
115947.e: The more people are in on it, the greater the risk that someone talks or evidence turns up. That is why big secrets can hardly be kept for long.
115947.m: The more people know, the harder it is to keep something secret.

115948.q: How does the Watergate affair in the USA differ from a conspiracy theory?
a: It took place in the Middle Ages
115948.e: In the early 1970s, journalists revealed that staff of President Nixon had carried out illegal actions. Courts and investigations confirmed this.
115948.m: Real conspiracies are uncovered with evidence that can be checked.

115949.q: What is a person or group called who is blamed for a misfortune without proof?
115949.e: Conspiracy stories often look for someone to blame for crises. Blaming people like this can lead to hatred of innocent people.
115949.m: A scapegoat is blamed for misfortune without proof.

a: A teaching that seems scientific but is not
A particularly new field of research
115950.e: “Pseudo” means false or pretended. Pseudosciences use technical words but do not follow methods that can be checked.
115950.m: Pseudoscience looks scientific but does not work that way.

115951.q: What does “cherry picking” mean with evidence?
a: Picking out only the data that fits
Collecting data as completely as possible
115951.e: As when picking cherries, you take only the best pieces. Data that does not fit is left out so that the result seems more convincing.
115951.m: Showing only data that fits is cherry picking.

115952.e: Science makes its methods public and can be checked. Pseudoscience often avoids tests or explains away failures afterwards.
115952.m: Avoiding checks is not working scientifically.

115954.q: Which 19th-century teaching wanted to read a person's character from the shape of their skull?
115954.e: Phrenology claimed that bumps on the skull revealed character traits. It was disproved and is seen as an example of pseudoscience.
115954.m: Phrenology could not read anything about character from skull shapes.

115955.q: Which historical teaching tried to turn base metals into gold?
115955.e: For centuries, alchemists searched for the “philosopher's stone”. They could not make gold, but their laboratory work helped chemistry to develop.

115956.q: Is there anything in the widespread belief that Mozart's music makes babies permanently more intelligent?
a: There is no evidence for it
It only works permanently in adults
It only works with classical music by Bach
115956.e: A study from 1993 found only a brief improvement in a spatial task among students. A lasting increase in babies' intelligence has never been shown.
115956.m: Listening to Mozart is fun but does not make you permanently cleverer.

a: Individual personal stories used as proof
115957.e: A sentence like “It helped my aunt” is an anecdote. Individual cases can be chance and therefore do not prove a general effect.
115957.m: Individual stories are not scientific proof.

115958.q: What is the difference between astronomy and astrology?
a: Astronomy studies heavenly bodies, astrology interprets fates
Astrology is the older name for space travel
115958.e: Astronomy is a natural science that measures and studies stars and planets. Astrology claims the stars influence people, for which there is no evidence.
115958.m: Astronomy is science, astrology is interpretation.

115959.q: How many signs of the zodiac does Western astrology have?
115959.e: Astrology divides the zodiac into twelve equal sections of 30 degrees each, from Aries to Pisces.
115959.m: Western astrology has twelve signs of the zodiac.

115960.q: Which constellation does the Sun also pass through, even though it is not a sign of the zodiac in astrology?
115960.e: Every year the Sun also passes through Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer, from about the end of November to mid-December. Astrology does not take it into account.
115960.m: The Sun travels through 13 constellations, not just 12.

115961.q: Why is the Sun on your birthday today usually no longer in the constellation of your own star sign?
a: The Earth's axis has slowly shifted over 2000 years
The Sun is getting faster and faster
115961.e: The Earth's axis wobbles very slowly like a spinning top. Since the star signs were fixed about 2000 years ago, the sky has therefore shifted by almost a whole constellation.
115961.m: Star signs and constellations no longer match today.

115962.q: Why do many people find their horoscope surprisingly accurate?
a: The statements are so general that they fit almost everyone
Horoscopes are measured for each person individually
115962.e: Sentences like “You are sometimes unsure of yourself” fit almost everyone. In an experiment, most students found the same text very accurate as their very own personal profile.
115962.m: General statements often seem surprisingly personal.

115963.q: What do scientific tests show in which astrologers have to match horoscopes to the right people?
a: Their hits are no better than chance
They are only right with children
They are only right at full moon
115963.e: In such blind tests, the astrologers do not know whose horoscope is whose. They are not right more often than by pure guessing.
115963.m: In controlled tests, astrology predicts no more than chance.

115964.q: What does a horoscope originally show?
a: The positions of the heavenly bodies at a point in time
The weather forecast for a week
The Sun's path around the Earth
115964.e: A horoscope is a drawing that records the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets, for example at birth. Astrology interprets character and fate from it.
115964.m: A horoscope shows the sky at a particular moment.

115965.q: Which famous astronomer also made horoscopes to earn money?
115965.e: Kepler discovered the laws of planetary orbits. Because horoscopes were in demand at the time, he also wrote them and partly paid his living costs that way.
115965.m: Even great astronomers used to write horoscopes for money.

115966.q: What do people want to find with a dowsing rod?
115966.e: Traditionally, people use a dowsing rod to search for underground water, ores or supposed “earth rays”.
115966.m: A dowsing rod is mainly used to search for water.

115967.q: What shape is a classic dowsing rod?
115967.e: The rod is held at both ends with tense hands. Modern rods are often bent wires or metal rods too.
115967.m: The classic dowsing rod is a forked branch.

115968.q: What are people called who search with a dowsing rod?
115968.e: Dowsers walk slowly across an area and watch for the rod to move. There is no scientifically recognised training for this.
115968.m: Someone who searches with a dowsing rod is called a dowser.

115969.q: What best explains why a dowsing rod moves?
115969.e: In the ideomotor effect, the muscles move very slightly without you noticing. The tense rod amplifies these small movements into a clear swing.
115969.m: The rod moves because of unconscious hand movements.

115970.q: Why do dowsers often seem successful when looking for water?
a: In many areas you find groundwater almost everywhere
115970.e: In central Europe, in many areas there is groundwater almost everywhere at a certain depth. A hit therefore does not prove that the rod works.
115970.m: Hits are no proof if you find water almost everywhere.

115971.q: How does groundwater usually occur in the ground?
a: In huge cave lakes under every town
115971.e: Groundwater usually fills the pores and cracks of gravel, sand or rock over large areas. Narrow “water veins”, as dowsers describe them, are the exception.
115971.m: Groundwater usually lies in wide layers, not narrow veins.

115972.q: How can you fairly test whether a person finds water with a dowsing rod?
a: With a blind test using hidden water pipes
115972.e: In a blind test, neither the person nor the observer knows which hidden pipe water is flowing through. Only this shows whether the hit rate is above chance.
115972.m: Only blind tests show whether an ability really exists.

115973.q: What happened to the one million dollar prize that the James Randi Educational Foundation offered for proof of supernatural abilities?
115973.e: Many applicants, including dowsers, came to be tested. None could show their ability under controlled conditions.
115973.m: Under controlled conditions, nobody could prove supernatural powers.

115974.q: Looked at closely, what shape is the Earth?
a: A sphere slightly flattened at the poles
115974.e: Because it spins, the Earth is a little wider at the equator than from pole to pole. The difference between the diameters is about 43 km.
115974.m: The Earth is slightly flattened at the poles.

115975.q: Which observation did Aristotle give as a sign that the Earth is round?
a: The round shadow of the Earth during lunar eclipses
115975.e: In a lunar eclipse, the Earth's shadow falls on the moon and is always round. Only a sphere casts a round shadow from every direction.
115975.m: The Earth's round shadow on the moon reveals its shape.

115976.q: What do you see when a ship at sea sails far away?
a: It disappears from the bottom up
It just gets smaller and smaller
It disappears from the top down
115976.e: Because of the Earth's curve, the hull disappears behind the horizon first and the top of the mast last. On a flat Earth, the ship would simply get smaller.
115976.m: Because of the Earth's curve, ships disappear from the bottom first.

115977.q: Is it true that scholars in the Middle Ages thought the Earth was a disc?
a: No, they knew it was round
Yes, they all thought it was flat
No, they thought it was a cube
115977.e: Since ancient times, educated people knew the Earth was a sphere. The idea that the Middle Ages believed in a disc is itself a myth from later times.
115977.m: Medieval scholars knew that the Earth is a sphere.

115978.q: What was the argument before Columbus's voyage in 1492 really about?
115978.e: Columbus thought the Earth was far too small and the route to Asia too short. His critics were right that Asia was too far away.
115978.m: Columbus was wrong about the size of the Earth, not its shape.

115979.q: Which expedition was the first to sail around the whole world, from 1519 to 1522?
115979.e: Ferdinand Magellan died on the way, but Juan Sebastián Elcano completed the voyage with one ship. The journey around the world confirmed in practice that the Earth is round.
115979.m: Magellan's expedition was the first to sail around the Earth.

115980.q: Why is it still early morning in New York when it is already midday in Zurich?
a: Because the Sun only lights up half of the spinning globe
Because New York is higher up
Because the clocks in the USA are wrong
Because the Sun is closer in Europe
115980.e: The Earth spins, and only one half of the globe faces the Sun at any time. That is why there are time zones, which could not be explained on a flat disc.
115980.m: Time zones exist because the Earth spins.

115981.q: Roughly how long is the Earth's circumference at the equator?
115981.e: The circumference at the equator is about 40,075 km. The metre was originally defined so that a quarter of a meridian is 10,000 km long.
115981.m: The Earth measures about 40,000 km around the equator.

115982.q: What do astronauts see from the ISS space station at a height of about 400 km?
a: The curved surface of the Earth
A wall of ice around the world
115982.e: From the ISS the horizon is clearly curved. The station circles the Earth about every 90 minutes.
115982.m: From space you can clearly see that the Earth is round.

115983.q: What do you do in a fact check?
a: You check whether a claim is true
115983.e: In a fact check, statements are compared with reliable sources and data. The result can be true, false or misleading.
115983.m: A fact check tests claims against evidence.

115984.q: How can you find out where and when a photo first appeared on the internet?
115984.e: In a reverse search, you upload the image to a search engine. This shows whether an old image is being spread again in the wrong context.
115984.m: A reverse image search shows where a photo comes from.

115985.q: A supposed quote from a famous person goes viral. What is a sensible step to check it?
a: Look for the original source of the quote
Look at the number of likes
115985.e: Many quotes are falsely put into the mouths of famous people. Only a book, speech or interview as a source shows whether someone really said it.
115985.m: A quote is only believable once you know its source.

115986.q: What is the best way to check an unfamiliar website?
a: Read what other sources say about it
See whether it is nicely designed
Believe it if it is at the top of the search results
115986.e: Instead of just staying on the site, you look in other tabs to see who is behind it. Professional fact-checkers work this way too.
115986.m: It is best to check a source from the outside.

115987.q: Which hidden information in a photo file can reveal when and with what a picture was taken?
115987.e: Cameras and phones often store the date, the device and sometimes the location in the file. But this metadata can also be missing or changed.
115987.m: Metadata reveals a lot about where a photo comes from.

115988.q: A risk rises from 1 to 2 cases per 10,000 people. By how much has the risk risen in absolute terms?
115988.e: 1 in 10,000 is 0.01 per cent, 2 in 10,000 is 0.02 per cent. So the rise is only 0.01 percentage points, even though the risk has “doubled”.
115988.m: Doubling can mean very little with small numbers.

115989.q: In summer, ice cream sales and swimming accidents rise at the same time. What follows from this?
a: Both have a common cause, the heat
Swimming accidents make you want ice cream
115989.e: Two things that rise together are not necessarily cause and effect. Here, the warm weather leads to more ice cream and more swimmers.
115989.m: Rising together does not prove a cause.

115990.q: Why should you read more than just the headline before sharing an article?
115990.e: A headline has to be short and eye-catching, so it often leaves out important things. Only the whole text shows what is really being claimed.
115990.m: Read the whole article before sharing it.

a: Checking the origin and credibility of a source
Rating a source as badly as possible
115991.e: In source criticism, you ask who wrote something, when, where and with what intention. Only then can you judge how reliable a piece of information is.
115991.m: Source criticism means checking where information comes from.

115992.q: A diary from 1940 is read in a history lesson. What kind of source is it?
115992.e: Primary sources come directly from the time being studied. A school book that reports on that time would be a secondary source.
115992.m: Primary sources come from the time in question.

115993.q: Where on a website do you find who is responsible for the content?
115993.e: Serious websites give the names and contact details of those responsible in the legal notice. If there is none, be careful.
115993.m: The legal notice shows who is behind a website.

115994.q: What is the best way to check a statement in a Wikipedia article?
115994.e: Wikipedia articles are supposed to back up their statements with evidence. The references lead you to the original source.
115994.m: On Wikipedia, it is worth looking at the references.

115995.q: What does the label “Ad” or “Sponsored” on a post mean?
115995.e: Such posts were paid for by a company. They are mainly meant to sell and are therefore not neutral.
115995.m: Sponsored posts are adverts and not neutral.

115996.q: A study on sugary drinks was paid for by a drinks maker. What should you pay special attention to?
115996.e: Whoever pays for a study often has an interest in a particular result. The study is not automatically wrong, but it should be checked especially carefully.
115996.m: With paid-for studies, check for conflicts of interest.

115997.q: Why is the publication date of a source important?
a: Older information can be out of date
115997.e: Figures, records or research results change over time. An old article may therefore no longer be true today.
115997.m: With every source, check how up to date it is.

115998.q: Which question is NOT one of the typical questions of source criticism?
a: How many likes does the post have?
With what intention was it made?
115998.e: The number of likes only shows how popular a post is, not whether it is true. What matters is the author, the time and the intention.

a: Checking of a study by independent experts
A rating in the app store
115999.e: Before a journal publishes a study, other experts read it critically. They look for mistakes and often ask for improvements.
115999.m: In peer review, experts check the work of other experts.

116000.q: What does the word “peer” mean in peer review?
116000.e: The reviewers are researchers from the same field. So they are “equals” of the authors.
116000.m: Peers are experts at the same level.

116001.q: What does double-blind peer review mean?
a: Reviewers and researchers do not know each other's names
The study is checked in the dark
116001.e: This is so that fame, friendship or rivalry does not influence the judgement. Only the work itself is assessed.
116001.m: In double-blind peer review, both sides stay anonymous.

116002.e: Preprints make results available quickly, for example during a crisis. But they have not yet been checked by experts, so they should be read with caution.
116002.m: Preprints are studies that have not yet been reviewed.

116003.q: What can peer review NOT guarantee?
a: That a result is definitely correct
116003.e: Reviewers only see the submitted manuscript and cannot repeat every experiment. Mistakes or even fraud can therefore go undetected.
116003.m: Peer review reduces mistakes, but does not make results infallible.

116004.q: What is it called when other researchers repeat an experiment to check the result?
116004.e: A result is considered especially reliable if independent teams confirm it several times. If it cannot be repeated, caution is needed.
116004.m: Repeated experiments make knowledge more certain.

116005.q: What happens to a published study if serious mistakes or deception are found later?
116005.e: In 2010, for example, the journal “The Lancet” withdrew a 1998 study that had claimed a false link between vaccination and autism.

116006.q: Which journal is a well-known example of a peer-reviewed journal?
116006.e: “Nature” has been published since 1869 and publishes research from all the natural sciences. Submitted papers are reviewed by experts.
116006.m: Major journals have studies checked before they are printed.

116007.q: What are publishers called that publish almost anything for payment without real review?
116007.e: Predatory publishers pretend to be serious academic journals but hardly check the papers. Their articles are therefore less trustworthy.
116007.m: Not every journal with a scientific name really checks.

116008.q: From which subunits does filamentous F-actin in muscle polymerise?
116008.e: F-actin forms when many globular G-actin molecules join together. The G stands for globular, the F for filamentous.
116008.m: Many globular G-actins together form an F-actin filament.

116009.q: Which thread-like protein lies in the groove of the actin filament and covers the binding sites for myosin at rest?
116009.e: Tropomyosin winds along the actin filament and blocks the myosin binding sites at rest. Only when calcium binds to troponin is it moved aside.
116009.m: At rest, tropomyosin blocks myosin's access to actin.

116010.q: Which ions must be released in the muscle cell for the muscle to contract?
116010.e: Calcium binds to troponin. This moves tropomyosin aside, and myosin can attach to actin.

116011.q: What is the smallest contractile unit of a muscle fibre, bounded by two Z discs, called?
116011.e: In the sarcomere, actin and myosin filaments are arranged regularly. When it contracts they slide past each other and the Z discs move closer together.
116011.m: The sarcomere is the smallest working unit of the muscle.

116012.q: Which protein forms the thick filaments in muscle that pull on the actin filaments?
116012.e: The heads of myosin bind to actin and, using ATP, pull it towards the middle of the sarcomere. This shortens the muscle.
116012.m: Myosin pulls on actin and so shortens the muscle.

116013.q: What is the explanation of muscle contraction called in which actin and myosin filaments slide past each other?
116013.e: The filaments themselves do not get shorter. They slide into each other, which shortens each sarcomere and so the whole muscle.
116013.m: During contraction, actin and myosin slide past each other.

116014.q: To which component of all body cells do actin filaments also belong outside muscle?
116014.e: As microfilaments, actin threads form part of the cytoskeleton. They stabilise the shape of the cell and make cell movement possible.
116014.m: Actin occurs as microfilaments in practically all cells.

116015.q: What shape does an actin filament have?
a: Two chains twisted around each other
A flat band of folded sheets
116015.e: An actin filament looks like two twisted strings of beads. The hollow cylinder of 13 protofilaments, by contrast, describes a microtubule.
116015.m: An actin filament looks like two twisted strings of beads.

116016.q: Which part of the myosin II molecule has ATPase activity?
116016.e: The head of myosin binds both actin and ATP and splits the ATP. The long tail is used to assemble into thick filaments.
116016.m: The myosin head is both motor and ATP-splitting enzyme.

116017.q: How is a myosin II molecule in muscle built?
a: A long tail with two heads
A chain of spheres without a head
116017.e: Two myosin chains twist into a long tail and end in two heads. Many such molecules assemble into thick filaments.
116017.m: Myosin II has two heads on a long tail.

116018.q: Which substance supplies the energy for the movement of the myosin heads?
116018.e: The myosin head splits ATP and uses the energy released to cock itself. In the power stroke it pulls the actin filament a bit further.
116018.m: Myosin heads move with energy from ATP.

116019.q: Does myosin form the thick or the thin filaments in the sarcomere?
116019.e: Many myosin molecules form the thick filaments in the middle of the sarcomere. The thin filaments consist mainly of actin.
116019.m: Myosin forms the thick filaments, actin the thin ones.

116020.q: Why does rigor mortis set in after death?
a: Without ATP, the myosin heads stay stuck to the actin
The calcium is completely broken down
The actin breaks down into G-actin
The muscle fills with lactate crystals
116020.e: Without ATP the cross-bridges can no longer detach, so actin and myosin stay firmly linked. The stiffness only wears off when the proteins decompose.
116020.m: Rigor mortis is a result of missing ATP.

116021.q: What does the sliding filament theory of muscle contraction state?
a: The filaments slide past each other without getting shorter themselves
The filaments contract like rubber bands
The muscle fibres get shorter by taking up water
The filaments dissolve with every contraction
116021.e: In 1954 several researchers showed that actin and myosin filaments keep their length. The muscle shortens because they slide further into each other.
116021.m: During contraction the filaments slide into each other.

116022.q: In which direction do the myosin heads pull the actin filaments during contraction?
a: Towards the middle of the sarcomere
116022.e: The myosin heads on both sides of the M line pull the actin filaments towards the middle of the sarcomere. This brings the Z discs closer together.
116022.m: During contraction the actin filaments slide towards the middle of the sarcomere.

116023.q: What are the connections between myosin heads and actin that form in cycles during contraction called?
116023.e: The myosin heads form temporary cross-bridges with the actin. Each cycle of binding, tilting and releasing uses one ATP.
116023.m: Myosin and actin connect via cross-bridges.

116024.q: Which structures bound a sarcomere at both ends?
116024.e: A sarcomere runs from one Z disc to the next. It is the smallest contractile unit of striated muscle.
116024.m: A sarcomere lies between two Z discs.

116025.q: What is the light area of the sarcomere called that contains only thin actin filaments?
116025.e: The I band contains only actin filaments and appears light (isotropic) under a polarising microscope. It is cut in half by the Z disc.
116025.m: The I band contains only actin filaments.

116026.q: What is the central area of the sarcomere called where only myosin filaments lie, without overlap with actin?
116026.e: The H zone contains myosin filaments but no actin filaments. During contraction it becomes narrower or disappears completely.
116026.m: The H zone is the actin-free middle of the sarcomere.

116027.q: Which section of the sarcomere stays the same length during contraction?
a: The distance between the Z discs
116027.e: The A band matches the length of the myosin filaments, which do not shorten. The I band and H zone get shorter because the filaments overlap more.
116027.m: The A band keeps its length during contraction.

116028.q: Roughly how long is a sarcomere in resting skeletal muscle?
116028.e: A resting sarcomere measures about 2 to 2.5 micrometres. Thousands of sarcomeres in a row form a myofibril.
116028.m: A sarcomere is only a few micrometres long.

116029.q: Which protein of the sarcomere is considered the largest known human protein?
116029.e: Titin reaches from the Z disc to the M line and acts like an elastic spring. Depending on the variant, it consists of about 27,000 to over 34,000 amino acids.
116029.m: Titin is the giant protein and the spring of the sarcomere.

116030.q: At what sarcomere length does a skeletal muscle produce the greatest force?
a: At medium length with optimal overlap
The force does not depend on length
116030.e: The force depends on the number of possible cross-bridges. With optimal overlap of actin and myosin there are the most, with strong stretching or compression fewer.
116030.m: The greatest force comes with optimal filament overlap.

116031.q: What is the structure in the middle of the sarcomere called where the myosin filaments are anchored?
116031.e: In the M line, proteins such as myomesin link the thick filaments together. It lies exactly in the middle of the A band.
116031.m: The M line holds the myosin filaments together in the middle of the sarcomere.

116032.q: Why does skeletal muscle look striated under the microscope?
a: The sarcomeres lie regularly side by side
The cell nuclei lie in rows
Connective tissue wraps around the fibres
116032.e: In all myofibrils the sarcomeres lie at the same level. So light I bands and dark A bands form a continuous striped pattern.
116032.m: The striations come from the exact arrangement of the sarcomeres.

116033.q: What is a motor end plate?
a: The synapse between motor neuron and muscle fibre
The end of a tendon at the bone
The connection between two heart muscle cells
116033.e: At the motor end plate a motor neuron passes its signal chemically to a skeletal muscle fibre. It is also called the neuromuscular junction.
116033.m: The motor end plate is the synapse between nerve and muscle.

116034.q: Which enzyme quickly breaks down acetylcholine at the motor end plate?
116034.e: Acetylcholinesterase splits the messenger substance in the synaptic cleft within milliseconds. This stops the muscle staying permanently excited. Some nerve poisons inhibit this enzyme.
116034.m: Acetylcholinesterase ends the signal at the end plate.

116035.q: What happens at the muscle fibre membrane when acetylcholine binds to its receptors?
a: Ion channels open and the membrane is depolarised
The membrane becomes impermeable to all ions
The muscle fibre makes acetylcholine itself
116035.e: The receptors are also ion channels. Mainly sodium flows in, the voltage across the membrane flips and triggers an action potential.
116035.m: Acetylcholine opens ion channels and excites the muscle fibre.

116036.q: What does every end plate potential normally trigger in the skeletal muscle fibre?
116036.e: The end plate potential is so large that it reliably crosses the threshold. This is called a high safety factor of transmission.
116036.m: At a healthy end plate, every signal leads to an action potential.

116037.q: Which disease is caused by autoantibodies against the acetylcholine receptors of the motor end plate?
116037.e: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies block and destroy the receptors. Typical is muscle weakness that increases with use.
116037.m: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease of the end plate.

116038.q: How does the arrow poison curare act at the motor end plate?
a: It inhibits the breakdown of acetylcholine
It opens the calcium channels permanently
It increases the release of acetylcholine
116038.e: Curare occupies the receptors without opening them. The muscles become limp and paralysed, including the breathing muscles.
116038.m: Curare causes limp paralysis by blocking receptors.

116039.q: How does botulinum toxin act at the motor end plate?
a: It prevents the release of acetylcholine
116039.e: Botulinum toxin splits proteins needed for the vesicles to fuse with the membrane. Without the transmitter the muscle stays limp.

116040.q: Which ions flowing into the nerve ending trigger the release of the transmitter at the end plate?
116040.e: The arriving action potential opens voltage-gated calcium channels. The incoming calcium triggers the exocytosis of the vesicles.
116040.m: Calcium is the start signal for exocytosis of the transmitter vesicles.

116041.q: What is a motor neuron together with all the muscle fibres it supplies called?
116041.e: All fibres of a motor unit contract at the same time. In eye muscles there are only a few fibres, in large leg muscles often hundreds to over a thousand.
116041.m: A motor unit consists of one motor neuron and its muscle fibres.

116042.q: Which enzyme breaks down acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft?
116042.e: Acetylcholinesterase splits acetylcholine into acetate and choline. This ends the excitation at the synapse very quickly.
116042.m: Acetylcholinesterase ends the action of acetylcholine.

116043.q: Where in the nerve cell is acetylcholine stored until it is released?
116043.e: Acetylcholine is packed into small vesicles in the nerve ending. When an action potential arrives, they fuse with the membrane and release the messenger into the cleft.
116043.m: Messenger substances are stored and released in vesicles.

116044.q: After the poison of which mushroom are the muscarinic acetylcholine receptors named?
116044.e: The poison muscarine was obtained from the fly agaric (Amanita muscaria) in 1869. It specifically activates one type of acetylcholine receptor, which is therefore called muscarinic.
116044.m: The muscarinic receptors are named after a fly agaric poison.

116045.q: What are substances such as acetylcholine called that carry signals at synapses from one nerve cell to the next?
116045.e: Neurotransmitters are released at the synapse and bind to receptors on the next cell. Acetylcholine was the first neurotransmitter to be discovered.

116046.q: What happens in poisoning with nerve agents that inhibit acetylcholinesterase?
a: Acetylcholine builds up and causes constant excitation
116046.e: Without breakdown, acetylcholine stays in the cleft and keeps exciting the receptors. Muscle twitching, cramps and finally paralysis follow.
116046.m: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors lead to constant excitation.

116047.q: At which junction does a nerve use acetylcholine to pass the command on to a skeletal muscle?
116047.e: At the motor end plate the nerve ending releases acetylcholine. It binds to receptors on the muscle fibre, which then contracts.
116047.m: At the motor end plate, acetylcholine controls the muscle.

116048.q: How does acetylcholine released by the vagus nerve change the heart rate?
116048.e: At the heart, acetylcholine acts through muscarinic receptors at the sinus node. In this way the parasympathetic nervous system slows the heartbeat.
116048.m: Acetylcholine from the vagus nerve slows the heart.

116049.q: What triggers the release of acetylcholine from the nerve ending?
a: The formation of new muscle fibres
A signal from the muscle's cell nucleus
116049.e: When an action potential reaches the nerve ending, calcium flows in. The vesicles then fuse with the membrane and release acetylcholine.
116049.m: An action potential triggers the release of the messenger substance.

116050.q: What building blocks make up an ATP molecule?
a: Adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups
Adenine, deoxyribose and two phosphate groups
Adenosine, glucose and three phosphate groups
Guanine, ribose and three phosphate groups
116050.e: ATP is a nucleotide made of the base adenine, the sugar ribose and three phosphate groups. The bonds between the phosphates are rich in energy.
116050.m: ATP consists of adenine, ribose and three phosphates.

116051.q: Under standard conditions, roughly how much free energy is released when ATP is hydrolysed to ADP and phosphate?
116051.e: The standard value is about minus 30.5 kJ per mole. In the cell the amount is even larger because of the concentrations.
116051.m: Splitting ATP releases about 30 kilojoules per mole.

116052.q: Roughly how long does the ATP stored in muscle last under maximum effort?
116052.e: Muscle stores only very little ATP directly. That is why it has to be constantly remade from creatine phosphate, glucose and fats.
116052.m: The muscle's direct ATP store is very small.

116053.q: In which organelles of the muscle fibre is most ATP made during aerobic energy production?
116053.e: The citric acid cycle and the respiratory chain take place in the mitochondria. Endurance-trained muscles have especially many mitochondria.
116053.m: Mitochondria are the power stations of the muscle cell.

116054.q: How many ATP molecules does anaerobic glycolysis yield net per molecule of glucose?
116054.e: Glycolysis produces 4 ATP, but 2 are used up at the start. That leaves a net 2 ATP per glucose.
116054.m: Glycolysis yields a net two ATP per glucose.

116055.q: Roughly how much ATP does an adult turn over per day?
116055.e: Because ATP is constantly split and rebuilt, the turnover adds up to dozens of kilograms per day. Only a small amount is present in the body at any time.
116055.m: ATP is recycled many thousands of times a day.

116056.q: Which substance in muscle very quickly supplies phosphate for making new ATP during short maximum effort?
116056.e: Creatine phosphate passes its phosphate group directly to ADP. This store lasts a few seconds, for example during a sprint.
116056.m: Creatine phosphate is the fastest supply of ATP.

116057.q: Which enzyme in the inner mitochondrial membrane makes most of the ATP?
116057.e: ATP synthase uses the proton gradient of the respiratory chain like a turbine. Part of the enzyme rotates and joins ADP to phosphate.
116057.m: ATP synthase works like a molecular rotary motor.

116058.q: Which enzyme transfers the phosphate group from creatine phosphate to ADP?
116058.e: Creatine kinase catalyses the reaction creatine phosphate plus ADP to creatine plus ATP. The reaction is reversible.
116058.m: Creatine kinase makes ATP from creatine phosphate.

116059.q: How quickly can creatine phosphate rebuild used-up ATP in muscle?
116059.e: Creatine phosphate passes its phosphate group directly to ADP (Lohmann reaction). This means new ATP is available almost immediately.
116059.m: Creatine phosphate supplies new ATP in fractions of a second.

116060.q: Roughly how long does the creatine phosphate store last under maximum effort?
116060.e: Creatine phosphate supplies energy very quickly, but the store is small. After a few seconds glycolysis increasingly takes over.
116060.m: Creatine phosphate only lasts for a few seconds of top performance.

116061.q: In which sport is the creatine phosphate store the most important energy source?
116061.e: Short, maximum efforts are mainly covered by ATP and creatine phosphate. This store is nowhere near enough for long distances.
116061.m: For short sprints, muscle mainly uses creatine phosphate.

116062.q: What is energy supply via creatine phosphate called in sports physiology?
116062.e: In this process no oxygen is used and no lactate is formed. That is why it is called anaerobic and alactic.
116062.m: Splitting creatine phosphate works without oxygen and without lactate.

116063.q: Which breakdown product of creatine is excreted by the kidneys and serves as a measure of kidney function?
116063.e: Creatine and creatine phosphate are constantly converted into creatinine in small amounts. If the creatinine level in the blood rises, the kidneys are filtering less well.
116063.m: A high creatinine level in the blood points to weak kidney function.

116064.q: Where does the creatine in our muscles come from?
a: The body makes it itself and takes it in with meat and fish
It forms only from sugar in the muscles
It is taken in only with dairy products
Gut bacteria supply it as a vitamin
116064.e: The kidneys and liver make creatine from amino acids. We also take it in with meat and fish; vegetarians often have somewhat smaller stores.
116064.m: Creatine is made by the body and taken in with meat and fish.

116065.q: What does a greatly raised level of creatine kinase in the blood usually indicate?
116065.e: Creatine kinase sits in muscle cells and gets into the blood when they are damaged. It is raised, for example, after a heart attack, injuries or very hard exercise.
116065.m: Creatine kinase in the blood is a marker of muscle damage.

116066.q: Roughly how high is the lactate concentration in the blood of a healthy person at rest?
116066.e: At rest the blood lactate level is usually between about 0.5 and 2 mmol per litre. Under maximum effort it can rise to over 15 mmol per litre.
116066.m: Even at rest the blood contains some lactate.

116067.q: How does lactate formation benefit anaerobic glycolysis?
116067.e: When pyruvate is converted to lactate, NADH is oxidised to NAD+. Without NAD+, glycolysis would come to a standstill.

116068.q: What is the cycle called in which lactate from muscle is rebuilt into glucose in the liver?
116068.e: Lactate travels through the blood to the liver, where it becomes glucose by gluconeogenesis. This glucose can return to the muscle.
116068.m: In the Cori cycle the liver recycles lactate into glucose.

116069.q: What is now considered the main cause of muscle soreness after exercise?
a: Small injuries in the muscle fibres
116069.e: Lactate is usually broken down within one to two hours, but muscle soreness only appears later. It is put down to tiny tears and inflammation.
116069.m: Muscle soreness is caused by micro-injuries, not by lactate.

116070.q: Which blood lactate value was classically set as the aerobic-anaerobic threshold?
116070.e: Mader's 4 mmol threshold was used in training planning for a long time. Today the threshold is often determined individually.
116070.m: Classically, the anaerobic threshold is 4 mmol of lactate per litre.

116071.q: Which tissues use lactate from the blood as a source of energy?
a: The heart and slow muscle fibres
116071.e: Lactate is not a waste product but a fuel. Heart muscle and oxidative fibres convert it into pyruvate and burn it in the mitochondria.
116071.m: Lactate can be used as fuel by the heart and muscles.

116072.q: How can the breakdown of lactate after hard exercise be speeded up?
a: By jogging gently to cool down
116072.e: With light movement, blood flow stays high and the muscles burn lactate. Lying completely still slows the breakdown.
116072.m: Active recovery breaks down lactate faster.

116073.q: In which running distance does anaerobic glycolysis with lactate formation play a particularly large role?
116073.e: High-intensity effort lasting about 30 seconds to 2 minutes is largely covered by anaerobic glycolysis. That is why 400 m runners reach very high lactate levels.
116073.m: In the 400 m, lactate rises especially sharply.

116074.q: What does a muscle spindle measure?
a: The length and stretch of the muscle
The oxygen content in the muscle
116074.e: Muscle spindles are stretch receptors that lie parallel to the working fibres. They report the muscle's length and how it changes.
116074.m: Muscle spindles report the stretch of the muscle to the spinal cord.

116075.q: Where are the muscle spindles located?
a: In skeletal muscle between the muscle fibres
In the tendon at the bone
In the skin over the muscle
