About 30 g per kg of water
About 300 g per kg of water
116304.e: 2000 g of dry matter divided by 600 kg of water gives 3.33 g per kg. Put the other way round, the plant needs 300 kg of water per kg of dry matter.
116304.m: Water use efficiency divides the biomass by the amount of water used.

116305.q: How does a higher CO2 concentration in the air usually affect the water use efficiency of plants?
a: It rises, because the stomata can be narrower
It always stays exactly the same
It falls, because more water evaporates
116305.e: With more CO2 in the air, more CO2 gets into the leaf for the same opening time. Plants often narrow their pores and lose less water.
116305.m: More CO2 in the air usually improves water use efficiency.

116306.q: Through which openings does a plant lose most of its water?
116306.e: The plant takes in CO2 through the stomata, but also gives off water vapour. That is why it always has to balance photosynthesis against saving water.
116306.m: CO2 gets in and water gets out through the stomata.

116307.q: Which irrigation method particularly improves water use efficiency in farming?
a: Drip irrigation directly at the roots
116307.e: With drip irrigation, water goes straight to the roots. Little unused water is lost through evaporation or seeping away.
116307.m: Drip irrigation delivers water sparingly right to the roots.

116408.q: In which layer of the skin are melanocytes mainly found?
a: In the lowest layer of the epidermis
In the subcutis near the fat tissue
116408.e: Melanocytes sit in the basal layer, the lowest layer of the epidermis. From there their extensions reach the skin cells above.
116408.m: Melanocytes lie in the lowest layer of the epidermis.

116410.q: In which organelles do melanocytes make the pigment melanin?
116410.e: Melanin forms in special membrane-bound organelles, the melanosomes. These are then passed on to the surrounding skin cells.

116411.q: Which hereditary condition occurs when melanocytes cannot make melanin?
116411.e: In albinism the enzyme tyrosinase, which starts melanin production, is usually missing. Skin, hair and eyes then have hardly any pigment. In vitiligo, by contrast, melanocytes are only lost later.
116411.m: In albinism the pigment melanin is missing.

116412.q: How do melanocytes pass their pigment on to the keratinocytes?
116412.e: Melanocytes have dendritic extensions through which they hand melanosomes directly to neighbouring keratinocytes. In this way one melanocyte supplies many skin cells at once.
116412.m: Melanocytes distribute their pigment through their dendrites.

116413.q: Why do people with dark skin not have clearly more melanocytes than people with light skin?
a: What matters is the amount and type of melanosomes
Their melanocytes lie deeper in the dermis
116413.e: The number of melanocytes is similar for all skin colours. Differences come from the size, number and melanin type of the melanosomes and how they are spread in the keratinocytes.
116413.m: Skin colour depends on how active the melanocytes are, not on their number.

116414.q: Why do you only get properly tanned a few days after sunbathing?
a: The melanocytes first have to make new melanin and pass it on
The skin first has to peel
The blood first has to bring the pigment
The sun cream first has to break down
116414.e: UV radiation stimulates the melanocytes to make more melanin. It takes a few days for it to be made and spread to the skin cells.
116414.m: A tan develops because melanocytes make new pigment.

116415.q: Which skin disease is caused by the loss of melanocytes in sharply defined patches of skin?
116415.e: In vitiligo, melanocytes are usually destroyed by an autoimmune reaction. The affected areas lose their pigment and become white.
116415.m: In vitiligo, melanocytes are missing in white patches.

116416.q: How do the melanosomes in keratinocytes protect the DNA in a particularly targeted way?
a: They settle like a cap over the cell nucleus
They build themselves into the cell membrane
They move into the cell nucleus
116416.e: In keratinocytes the melanosomes gather on the side of the nucleus facing the sun. This nuclear cap absorbs UV radiation before it reaches the DNA.
116416.m: Melanin forms a sunshade for the DNA over the cell nucleus.

116417.q: How does UVA radiation differ from UVB radiation?
a: UVA has a longer wavelength and less energy
UVA has a shorter wavelength and more energy
UVA is part of visible light
UVA is completely filtered out by the ozone layer
116417.e: UVA ranges from 315 to 400 nanometres and borders on visible violet. UVB has a shorter wavelength and so more energy.
116417.m: UVA is the UV radiation with the longest wavelength.

116418.q: Roughly what share of the UV radiation reaching the ground is UVA?
116418.e: The ozone layer strongly filters short-wave UV radiation but hardly filters long-wave UVA. That is why most UV radiation at ground level is UVA.
116418.m: Almost all UV radiation at ground level is UVA.

116419.q: Down to which layer of the skin does UVA radiation mainly penetrate?
116419.e: Because of its longer wavelength, UVA gets deeper into the skin than UVB and reaches the dermis. There it damages collagen and elastic fibres.
116419.m: UVA penetrates down to the dermis.

116420.q: Which skin change is mainly caused by UVA radiation?
116420.e: UVA destroys collagen and elastic fibres in the dermis. In the long term this leads to wrinkles and leathery skin, known as photoageing.
116420.m: UVA makes the skin age prematurely.

116421.q: Why can you still get UV damage behind an ordinary window pane?
a: Normal glass lets through a lot of UVA
116421.e: Window glass largely blocks UVB but lets a large part of UVA radiation through. That is why behind glass sunburn is unlikely but skin ageing is possible.
116421.m: Behind normal glass, UVA still has an effect.

116422.q: How does UVA radiation mainly damage DNA?
116422.e: DNA absorbs UVA only weakly. However, UVA produces free radicals and other reactive oxygen compounds that damage the genetic material by oxidation.
116422.m: UVA damages DNA mainly through free radicals.

116423.q: Which type of radiation is dominant in the lamps of most sunbeds?
116423.e: Sunbeds tan mainly with UVA radiation, often with a small amount of UVB. The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies sunbed use as carcinogenic.

116424.q: Which rule applies in the EU to sunscreens with the circled UVA logo?
a: The UVA protection is at least one third of the SPF
The UVA protection is as high as the SPF
The product protects only against UVA
The product contains no chemical filters
116424.e: According to an EU recommendation, only products whose UVA protection reaches at least one third of the stated sun protection factor may carry the UVA logo. This ensures balanced protection.
116424.m: The UVA logo guarantees balanced UVA protection.

116425.q: Which UV radiation is largely, but not completely, held back by the ozone layer?
116425.e: UVB, at 280 to 315 nanometres, is strongly weakened by the ozone layer, but some of it reaches the ground. UVC is completely absorbed, UVA hardly at all.

116426.q: Which acute skin reaction is mainly triggered by UVB radiation?
116426.e: UVB has more energy than UVA and is strongly absorbed in the epidermis. There it triggers inflammation with redness: sunburn.
116426.m: Sunburn is mainly a result of UVB.

116427.q: Which DNA damage is typical of the direct effect of UVB?
116427.e: UVB is absorbed directly by DNA. Neighbouring pyrimidine bases such as thymine join together into dimers, which can cause mutations when the DNA is copied.
116427.m: UVB sticks neighbouring DNA bases together into dimers.

116428.q: Which protective reaction of the epidermis is triggered by repeated UVB exposure?
116428.e: UVB stimulates keratinocytes to divide and the horny layer becomes thicker. This so-called light callus scatters and absorbs part of the radiation.
116428.m: Repeated sun makes the horny layer thicker.

116429.q: What is the job of the protective protein p53, which is often damaged by UVB in skin cancer cells?
a: It stops cell division when DNA is damaged
It makes the skin pigment melanin
It transports oxygen into the skin
It builds collagen in the dermis
116429.e: p53 is considered the guardian of the genome: when DNA is damaged it halts cell division or makes the cell die. If it fails because of mutations, damaged cells can divide unchecked.
116429.m: The protective gene p53 is often damaged by UVB.

116430.q: How can researchers tell that a skin tumour was caused by UV radiation?
a: From typical mutation patterns in the DNA
From the colour of the tumour cells
From the temperature of the tumour
From the size of the cell nuclei
116430.e: UVB joins neighbouring DNA bases. During repair or copying, typical errors often occur, for example cytosine is replaced by thymine. This “UV signature” reveals the origin.
116430.m: Cytosine-to-thymine mutations are a fingerprint of UV radiation.

116431.q: When does the redness of sunburn typically reach its peak?
116431.e: The inflammation takes time, because messenger substances widen the blood vessels only gradually. The redness begins after a few hours and is usually strongest after about half a day to a full day.
116431.m: Sunburn only shows its full extent hours later.

116432.q: How is the UV index calculated from solar radiation?
a: From the irradiance weighted by its sunburn effect
From the air temperature at midday
From the number of hours of sunshine per day
From the brightness of visible light
116432.e: The UV radiation is weighted with the erythema action spectrum, in which UVB counts especially strongly. One index level corresponds to 25 milliwatts of erythemally effective radiation per square metre.
116432.m: The UV index measures radiation that causes sunburn.

116433.q: Why is a single UVB photon more dangerous for DNA than a UVA photon?
a: It carries more energy because of its shorter wavelength
It only has an effect at night
116433.e: The energy of a photon is inversely proportional to its wavelength. The more energetic UVB photons are also absorbed right in the range where DNA absorbs light.
116433.m: The shorter the wavelength, the more energetic the photon.

116434.q: Which skin cancer is the most common type of cancer of all in people with fair skin?
116434.e: Basal cell carcinoma, also called basalioma, is the most common malignant tumour in people with fair skin. It usually grows slowly.
116434.m: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common cancer in people with fair skin.

116435.q: What is typical of the way a basal cell carcinoma grows?
a: It destroys locally but rarely forms metastases
It spreads to the lungs very early
It grows only in mucous membranes
116435.e: Basal cell carcinoma can destroy surrounding tissue down to the bone. However, it only very rarely forms secondary tumours, which is why it is sometimes called semi-malignant.
116435.m: A basalioma grows destructively but hardly spreads.

116436.q: On which part of the body do basal cell carcinomas occur most often?
116436.e: Most basaliomas develop in places that get a lot of sun over decades, especially the face. The nose, forehead and ears are typical.
116436.m: Basaliomas usually develop on the sun-exposed face.

116437.q: What does a nodular basal cell carcinoma typically look like?
a: A glassy lump with a pearly edge and fine little blood vessels
A black spot with a ragged edge
116437.e: Typical are a skin-coloured to reddish, glassy shiny lump and a raised edge like a string of pearls. Widened blood vessels are often visible on the surface.
116437.m: A basalioma often shows a pearly raised edge.

116438.q: Which kind of UV exposure is considered the most important risk factor for basal cell carcinoma?
a: The UV dose built up over a lifetime
116438.e: The risk rises with the UV dose added up over a lifetime. That is why older people and people who work outdoors a lot are especially affected.
116438.m: For basalioma, the total UV dose of a lifetime counts.

116439.q: What does UV radiation do in skin cells that can lead to skin cancer such as basal cell carcinoma?
a: It fills the cells with water
It uses up all the melanin
116439.e: UV radiation changes building blocks of DNA. If the damage is not repaired, mutations arise and a cell can divide uncontrollably.
116439.m: Skin cancer is caused by UV damage to DNA.

116440.q: What is the standard treatment for a basal cell carcinoma?
116440.e: The basalioma is usually cut out completely. Microscopic examination of the cut edges checks whether the tumour has been fully removed.

116441.q: Why are the cut edges examined under the microscope after a basal cell carcinoma has been cut out?
a: To check whether the tumour has been completely removed
To count bacteria in the wound
116441.e: If tumour cells remain at the edge, the cancer can grow back. That is why more is cut away until the edges are free of tumour.
116441.m: Tumour-free edges show that the cancer has been completely removed.

116442.q: Why is a melanoma that grows quickly downwards particularly dangerous?
a: It quickly reaches blood and lymph vessels
It grows only on the scalp
It can never be operated on
116442.e: Blood and lymph vessels lie in the deeper dermis. The deeper a melanoma reaches, the more easily tumour cells can travel through them to other organs.
116442.m: The deeper a melanoma grows, the more dangerous it is.

116443.q: What does the “E” stand for in the ABCDE rule for assessing moles?
116443.e: The rule checks asymmetry, border, colour, diameter and evolution. A mole that changes in size, shape or colour should be examined by a doctor.
116443.m: A mole that changes should be checked by a doctor.

116444.q: From which cells does a melanoma develop?
a: From the pigment cells of the skin
From the fat cells of the subcutis
116444.e: A melanoma is a malignant tumour of the melanocytes, the cells that make the pigment melanin. That is why it is often dark in colour.
116444.m: A melanoma is a tumour of the pigment cells.

116445.q: Why is melanoma also called “black skin cancer” in German?
a: Because it is usually darkly pigmented
Because it occurs only on dark skin
Because it grows mainly at night
116445.e: Melanomas develop from pigment cells and often make a lot of melanin. That is why they usually look brown to black, unlike the light-coloured skin cancers.
116445.m: Melanomas are usually dark because they develop from pigment cells.

116446.q: Why should you also check the soles of your feet and your nails for unusual dark spots?
a: Melanomas can also develop in places that get little sun
There are no pigment cells there
The skin there is immune to cancer
116446.e: Not every melanoma is caused by the sun. One form grows on the palms, soles or under the nails, and in people with dark skin it is even the most common.
116446.m: Melanomas can also develop on the soles of the feet and under the nails.

116447.q: What lies behind the development of a melanoma at the level of the cell?
a: Changes in the DNA of the pigment cells
Too much melanin in the blood
116447.e: UV radiation can damage the DNA of pigment cells. If such mutations build up, for example in the BRAF gene, the cells divide uncontrollably.
116447.m: Melanomas are caused by DNA damage, often from UV radiation.

116448.q: Which treatment has greatly improved the chances in melanoma that has spread since the 2010s?
a: Immunotherapies that activate the immune system against the tumour
116448.e: New immunotherapies release a brake on the immune system. This allows T cells to attack the tumour cells more effectively.
116448.m: Immunotherapies help the immune system fight melanoma cells.

116449.q: What is a sentinel lymph node biopsy for in melanoma?
a: To check whether tumour cells have spread into the lymph system
116449.e: The sentinel lymph node is the first lymph node in the area that drains the tumour. If it is free of tumour cells, spread through the lymph is unlikely.
116449.m: The sentinel lymph node shows whether a melanoma has spread.

116450.q: Which factor raises the risk of melanoma particularly clearly?
a: Many moles and sunburns in childhood
Swimming often in an indoor pool
116450.e: A high number of moles and bad sunburns at a young age are among the most important risk factors. Fair skin and cases in the family also raise the risk.
116450.m: Sunburns in childhood raise the risk of melanoma.

116451.q: Which instrument do dermatologists use to examine moles magnified and lit up?
116451.e: The dermatoscope works with magnification and incident light. This makes structures in the skin visible that cannot be seen with the naked eye.
116451.m: With a dermatoscope you can see moles more closely.

116452.q: What does the “ugly duckling sign” mean when checking the skin?
a: A mole that looks different from all the others is suspicious
Moles on the hands are harmless
116452.e: Most of a person's moles look alike. A mole that does not fit the pattern, an ugly duckling, should be examined more closely.
116452.m: A mole that stands out from the rest should be checked.

116453.q: Which form of prevention does early detection of skin cancer belong to?
116453.e: Early detection means finding a disease that has already developed as early as possible. At this stage it can usually be treated well.

116454.q: Which measure belongs to the primary prevention of skin cancer?
a: Protection with clothing, a hat and shade
116454.e: Primary prevention aims to stop a disease from developing at all. For skin cancer this mainly means reducing UV exposure.
116454.m: The best protection against skin cancer is less UV radiation.

a: Specialists assessing skin images from a distance
Treating the skin with television light
A skin check only by phone without images
Measuring skin temperature from a distance
116455.e: In teledermatology, photos or dermatoscope images are sent electronically to specialists. They can then judge whether an examination in person is needed.
116455.m: Teledermatology assesses skin images from a distance.

116456.q: Which simple shadow rule helps you recognise the time of high UV exposure?
a: If your shadow is shorter than you are, look for shade
If your shadow is longer than you are, put on cream
Without a shadow there is no UV radiation
116456.e: A short shadow means the sun is high. Then the path through the atmosphere is short and UV radiation is correspondingly strong.
116456.m: A short shadow warns of strong UV radiation.

116457.q: After removal, how is a suspicious skin finding reliably confirmed or ruled out as cancer?
116457.e: The removed tissue is examined under the microscope in histology. Only this finding gives a confirmed diagnosis.
116457.m: Histology confirms the diagnosis of skin cancer.

116458.q: Why is a mirror or a second person useful when checking your own skin?
a: Because the back and scalp are otherwise hard to see
Because moles look bigger in the mirror
Because light would otherwise change the moles
Because it shows your blood group
116458.e: Skin cancer can develop anywhere, including places that are hard to see. With a mirror or help, you can check your back, neck and scalp.
116458.m: Self-checks should include places that are hard to see.

116459.q: Why should an actinic keratosis be treated?
a: It can develop into skin cancer
116459.e: Actinic keratoses are precancerous lesions. Without treatment they can turn into a light-coloured skin cancer.
116459.m: An actinic keratosis is a precancerous lesion.

116460.q: How does an actinic keratosis typically feel?
116460.e: The patches are often scaly and horny. They can often be felt better than seen.

116461.q: Where do actinic keratoses occur particularly often?
a: On a bald head, the forehead and the backs of the hands
On the soles of the feet
116461.e: The changes develop where the skin gets a lot of UV radiation over years. Typical places are a hairless scalp, the face, ears and the backs of the hands.
116461.m: Actinic keratoses grow in places plagued by the sun.

116462.q: What is the main trigger of actinic keratoses?
a: Chronic UV exposure over many years
A virus from the swimming pool
116462.e: The word actinic means caused by radiation. Years of sun exposure damage the DNA of the keratinocytes.
116462.m: Actinic keratoses are the result of years of sun exposure.

116463.q: Which treatment is often used for single actinic keratoses?
116463.e: In cryotherapy the patch is frozen with liquid nitrogen. The damaged cells die and healthy skin grows back.
116463.m: Single keratoses can be frozen off.

116464.q: What does the term “field cancerisation” mean for actinic keratoses?
a: The whole sun-damaged area of skin is altered
The cancer only grows on fields
Only one single spot is affected
116464.e: Besides the visible patches, the whole surrounding skin is often already UV-damaged. That is why whole areas are often treated instead of just single spots.
116464.m: In field cancerisation a whole area of skin is damaged.

116465.q: How does photodynamic therapy work for actinic keratoses?
a: An applied substance makes diseased cells sensitive to light, and light destroys them
UVB light turns the keratoses brown
116465.e: A cream with aminolevulinic acid builds up in the altered cells. When light is shone on them, reactive oxygen compounds form that kill these cells.
116465.m: In photodynamic therapy, light destroys marked precancerous cells.

116466.q: Which occupational group has a particularly high risk of actinic keratoses?
a: People who work outdoors a lot
People who work in an office at night
People who work in a laboratory
116466.e: Anyone who works, for example, in construction, farming or as a mountain guide is exposed to strong sunlight for years. In Germany, multiple actinic keratoses and squamous cell carcinomas caused by UV radiation have therefore been recognised as an occupational disease since 2015.
116466.m: People who work outdoors need especially good sun protection.

116467.q: How do mineral UV filters such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide work?
a: They scatter, reflect and absorb UV radiation
116467.e: Mineral filters are fine particles that reflect, scatter and partly absorb UV radiation. They are considered well tolerated but can leave a white film.
116467.m: Mineral filters protect with tiny particles on the skin.

116468.q: What happens to the energy that organic UV filters absorb?
a: It is mostly given off as heat
It is converted into vitamin D
It is given off again as UVC
It is stored in the filter
116468.e: Organic filter molecules absorb UV photons and enter an excited state. When they fall back, they give off the energy mostly as heat.
116468.m: Organic UV filters turn UV energy into heat.

116469.q: How is the sun protection factor defined?
a: As the ratio of the sunburn threshold with and without sunscreen
As the share of infrared radiation blocked
As the number of hours of protection per application
As the amount of filter in grams per tube
116469.e: The SPF compares the UV dose that causes minimal redness with sunscreen to the dose without protection. An SPF of 20 means that about twenty times the dose is needed.
116469.m: The sun protection factor tells you how many times more UVB the skin can tolerate.

116470.q: Roughly what share of UVB radiation does a sunscreen with SPF 30 hold back when used correctly?
116470.e: With SPF 30, about one thirtieth of the radiation reaches the skin, so just over 3 per cent. About 97 per cent is blocked.

116471.q: Why do many people not reach the sun protection factor stated on the pack in everyday life?
a: They put on too little sun cream
They put cream on in the shade
116471.e: In the lab the sun protection factor is measured with 2 milligrams per square centimetre of skin. In everyday life most people only use a fraction of that, which clearly lowers the protection.
116471.m: If you apply too thinly, you do not get the stated protection.

116472.q: Does reapplying sunscreen on the same day extend the total protection time beyond the original?
a: No, it only maintains the protection
116472.e: Reapplying replaces sunscreen that has been rubbed or washed off. However, the maximum protection time, which comes from the skin's own protection time and the SPF, is not extended.
116472.m: Reapplying maintains protection but does not extend it.

116473.q: Which US state was the first to ban sunscreens with the filters oxybenzone and octinoxate to protect coral reefs?
116473.e: In 2018 Hawaii decided to ban the sale of sunscreens with these two filters. The ban came into force in 2021 because the substances might harm corals.
116473.m: Some UV filters are suspected of harming corals.

116474.q: Why is titanium dioxide often used as nanoparticles in sun creams?
a: Finer particles leave less of a white film
116474.e: Large pigment particles also scatter visible light and make the skin look white. Very small particles are almost transparent but still filter UV.
116474.m: Nanoparticles make mineral sun cream more transparent.

116475.q: In the EU, what is the highest permitted sun protection factor label on sunscreens?
116475.e: According to an EU recommendation, products with very high protection are labelled “50+”. Higher numbers would suggest an extra benefit that hardly exists.
116475.m: The highest sun protection factor on EU labels is 50+.

116476.q: What causes the immediate pigmentation shortly after UVA exposure?
a: Melanin already present is oxidised and darkens
Blood builds up in the skin
116476.e: In immediate pigmentation no new melanin is made. Existing pigment precursors are oxidised by UVA, and the colour usually fades again quickly.
116476.m: The immediate tan only darkens pigment that is already there.

116477.q: After how long does the delayed tan from newly formed melanin become visible?
116477.e: In delayed pigmentation the melanocytes make new melanin and pass it on to the keratinocytes. This process takes a few days.
116477.m: A real tan only develops after a few days.

116478.q: Roughly how much protection does a well-developed suntan give?
a: About the same as a sun protection factor of 2 to 4
About the same as a sun protection factor of 30
About the same as a sun protection factor of 50
116478.e: A tan offers only slight natural protection. It does not replace sun cream, clothing or shade.
116478.m: Tanned skin is only weakly protected against UV.

116479.q: From a biological point of view, what does a tan show?
a: A reaction to UV damage in the skin
116479.e: Tanning is triggered when UV radiation damages the DNA of keratinocytes. Through signalling substances these cells stimulate the melanocytes to make pigment.
116479.m: A tan is a sign that the skin is defending itself against damage.

116480.q: Which cells in the skin make the pigment melanin?
116480.e: Melanocytes sit in the lowest layer of the epidermis. They make melanin and pass it on to the surrounding skin cells, which become darker as a result.
116480.m: Melanocytes make the skin pigment melanin.

116481.q: Which active ingredient in self-tanners colours the horny layer without UV radiation?
116481.e: Dihydroxyacetone reacts with amino acids in the top layer of skin to form brown compounds. This colour does not protect against UV radiation and disappears as the skin flakes off.
116481.m: Self-tanners colour the skin but do not protect against the sun.

116482.q: Which rule applies in Switzerland to the use of sunbeds by minors?
a: It is only allowed with sun cream
It is only allowed in winter
116482.e: Under the Federal Act on Protection against Dangers from Non-Ionising Radiation and Sound, young people under 18 may not use sunbeds. Their skin is considered particularly sensitive.
116482.m: In Switzerland, sunbeds are banned for minors.

116483.q: Which fashion designer is considered to have made the suntan an ideal of beauty in the 1920s?
116483.e: Before that, pale skin was considered refined in Europe. Coco Chanel appeared with a tan, and a tan became a sign of leisure and wealth.
116483.m: A tan only became an ideal of beauty in the 20th century.

116484.q: Why is it useful to know your own skin type?
a: To calculate your vitamin C needs
116484.e: The skin type shows how sensitively the skin reacts to sun. If you know it, you can adapt sun cream, clothing and time in the sun better.
116484.m: Your skin type helps you choose the right sun protection.

116485.q: How many skin types does the Fitzpatrick scale distinguish?
116485.e: The scale ranges from type I with very fair skin that always burns to type VI with deeply dark skin. There are four more levels in between.
116485.m: The Fitzpatrick scale has six skin types.

116486.q: Which feature describes Fitzpatrick skin type I?
a: Always burns and practically never tans
116486.e: People with skin type I have very fair skin, often freckles and reddish hair. They have the shortest natural protection time.
116486.m: Skin type I burns quickly and hardly tans.

116487.q: By which criterion are Fitzpatrick skin types mainly classified?
a: By how the skin reacts to sun
By the fat content of the skin
By the number of hairs per cm²
116487.e: What matters is how easily the skin gets sunburnt and how well it tans. From this its sensitivity to light can be estimated.
116487.m: Skin types describe how sensitive the skin is to sun.

116488.q: What does the term “natural protection time” of the skin mean?
a: The time without protection until sunburn begins
The time until the skin grows back
The time until sun cream soaks in
The time until a tan fades
116488.e: The natural protection time tells you how long unprotected skin can be exposed to the sun before it turns red. It depends on skin type and the UV index.
116488.m: The natural protection time is especially short for fair skin.

116489.q: A person has a natural protection time of 10 minutes and uses SPF 30 correctly. What is the theoretical maximum protection time?
116489.e: You multiply the natural protection time by the sun protection factor: 10 minutes times 30 makes 300 minutes. Experts recommend using only about two thirds of this time.
116489.m: Protection time is natural protection time times sun protection factor.

116490.q: Which skin types are especially common among people in Switzerland of central European origin?
116490.e: Many people of central European origin have fair to medium-fair skin that first burns and then tans. This corresponds to skin types II and III.
116490.m: In central Europe, skin types II and III are most common.

116491.q: Can people with skin type VI get skin cancer?
116491.e: Dark skin is better protected against UV, but not completely. In dark skin, skin cancer is also often detected late, for example on the soles of the feet.
116491.m: Even very dark skin can develop skin cancer.

116492.q: Which group of cells do the Langerhans cells of the skin belong to?
a: Dendritic cells of the immune system
Muscle cells of the hair follicle muscles
116492.e: Langerhans cells are antigen-presenting immune cells of the epidermis. With their extensions they form a dense surveillance network.
116492.m: Langerhans cells are the immune system's guards in the epidermis.

116493.q: What did Paul Langerhans first think the cells he discovered in the epidermis in 1868 were?
116493.e: Paul Langerhans described the branched cells in 1868 as a young medical student. Because of their extensions he thought they were nerve cells; their role in the immune system was only recognised about a hundred years later.
116493.m: Langerhans cells were first thought to be nerve cells.

116494.q: How do Langerhans cells keep watch over the whole epidermis even though there are only a few of them?
a: By forming a horny layer themselves
116494.e: Langerhans cells stretch their extensions out between the skin cells and so form a dense network. Under the electron microscope they can also be recognised by the tennis-racket-shaped Birbeck granules.
116494.m: Langerhans cells form a surveillance network with their extensions.

116495.q: What do Langerhans cells do after they have taken up a foreign antigen?
a: They travel to the lymph nodes and present it to T cells
They dissolve in the horny layer
116495.e: The cells process the antigen and travel through lymph vessels to the lymph nodes. There they activate T lymphocytes and start a targeted defence.
116495.m: Langerhans cells take foreign substances to the T cells.

116496.q: What effect does UV radiation have on Langerhans cells?
a: It reduces their number and function
It turns them into fat cells
116496.e: UV radiation weakens Langerhans cells and so suppresses the immune defence in the skin. This makes it easier for damaged cells to escape immune control.
116496.m: UV radiation weakens the skin's immune system.

116497.q: How are Langerhans cells made specifically visible in a skin sample under the microscope?
a: With labelled antibodies against their surface molecules
With a magnifying glass and no staining at all
116497.e: Langerhans cells carry typical molecules such as CD1a and langerin. Labelled antibodies bind to them and stain the cells specifically.
116497.m: Labelled antibodies are used to stain particular cells specifically.

116498.q: Which structures should Langerhans cells of the skin not be confused with, even though they have the same discoverer?
a: Islets of Langerhans in the pancreas
116498.e: Paul Langerhans also described groups of cells in the pancreas that make hormones such as insulin. These have nothing to do with the immune cells of the skin.
116498.m: Langerhans cells and islets of Langerhans are different things.

116499.q: In which part of the skin are Langerhans cells mainly found?
a: In the bone marrow of the skin
116499.e: Langerhans cells sit mainly in the middle layers of the epidermis. There they catch pathogens and foreign substances that get past the horny layer.
116499.m: Langerhans cells keep watch over the epidermis.

116500.q: Which layer of skin forms the most important physical barrier against water loss?
116500.e: The horny layer consists of dead, keratinised cells embedded in lipids. It stops the body losing too much water.
116500.m: The horny layer is the skin's most important barrier.

116501.q: Which model gives a clear picture of how the horny layer is built?
116501.e: The keratinised cells are the bricks, the lipids between them the mortar. Together they make a tight wall.
116501.m: The horny layer is built like a wall of bricks and mortar.

116502.q: Which group of lipids makes up a main share of the barrier lipids in the horny layer?
116502.e: The lipids between the horny cells consist mainly of ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids. They arrange themselves in dense layers.
116502.m: Ceramides are important building blocks of the skin barrier.

116503.q: Roughly what pH does the acid mantle of healthy skin surface have?
116503.e: The skin surface is slightly acidic, roughly in the range pH 4.5 to 5.5. This inhibits many pathogens and supports enzymes that build the barrier.
116503.m: Healthy skin is slightly acidic on the surface.

116504.q: Which skin disease is closely linked to a disturbed skin barrier?
116504.e: In atopic eczema the skin barrier is weakened. The skin loses a lot of water, becomes dry and reacts sensitively to irritants and allergens.
116504.m: Atopic eczema goes together with a disturbed skin barrier.

116505.q: Which measurement is often used to test the function of the skin barrier?
116505.e: Transepidermal water loss measures how much water evaporates outwards through the skin. If the barrier is damaged, this value rises.
116505.m: A lot of water loss through the skin shows a disturbed barrier.

116506.q: Roughly how long does it take for the epidermis to renew itself from the basal layer to flaking off?
116506.e: New cells form in the basal layer, move upwards and become keratinised. After about four weeks they flake off at the surface.
116506.m: The epidermis renews itself about once a month.

116507.q: Why can washing very often with soap weaken the skin barrier?
a: It dissolves lipids and shifts the pH
116507.e: Surfactants dissolve skin fats out of the horny layer, and alkaline soaps raise the pH. The skin becomes dry and more prone to irritation.
116507.m: Too much soap removes the skin's fats and weakens its barrier.

116508.q: The gravitational force F acts between two bodies. One mass is tripled and the distance halved. What is the new force?
116508.e: Triple the mass gives a factor of 3, half the distance a factor of 1/(1/2)² = 4. Together this gives 3 times 4, so 12 F.
116508.m: Masses enter the gravitational force simply, distances squared.

116509.q: How does the gravitational force change if you double both masses and keep the distance the same?
a: It becomes four times as large
It becomes eight times as large
116509.e: The force is proportional to the product of the two masses. If you double both, the product becomes 2 times 2, so four times as large.
116509.m: Gravitational force grows with the product of the masses.

116510.q: Under what condition can extended celestial bodies be treated as point masses at their centres in the law of gravitation?
a: When they are the same size
When they are made of rock
116510.e: Newton proved that a spherically symmetrical mass acts outwards as if all its mass were concentrated at its centre. That is why the distance r is measured from centre to centre.
116510.m: Spheres attract as if their mass were at the centre.

116511.q: An apple falls from a tree. How large is the force with which the apple pulls the Earth compared with the force of the Earth on the apple?
116511.e: According to Newton’s third law, force and counterforce are equal and opposite. The Earth hardly moves only because of its huge mass.
116511.m: The apple and the Earth attract each other with equal force.

116512.q: Roughly what is the gravitational force between the Earth and the Moon?
116512.e: With F = G·m1·m2/r², the Earth’s mass of 5.97·10^24 kg, the Moon’s mass of 7.34·10^22 kg and a distance of 3.84·10^8 m, the result is about 1.98·10^20 newtons.
116512.m: The Earth and the Moon attract each other with about 2·10^20 newtons.

116513.q: The Moon is about 60 Earth radii from the centre of the Earth. What fraction of g did Newton therefore expect for its centripetal acceleration?
116513.e: At 60 times the distance, the acceleration falls to 1/60², so 1/3600 of g. That gives about 2.7 mm/s², which matches the observed orbit of the Moon.
116513.m: Newton tested his law on the orbit of the Moon.

116514.q: Which observation could Newton’s law of gravitation not fully explain?
a: The orbital period of the Moon
116514.e: Mercury’s perihelion shifts slightly faster than Newton’s theory predicts, even including all disturbances. Only Einstein’s general theory of relativity of 1915 explained the remaining approximately 43 arcseconds per century.
116514.m: Mercury’s orbit showed the limits of Newton’s theory.

116515.q: The distance between two bodies is tripled. To what fraction does the gravitational force fall?
116515.e: The force depends on 1/r². At three times the distance this gives 1/3², so one ninth of the original force.
116515.m: Three times the distance means one ninth of the force.

116516.q: Why do a feather and a hammer fall at the same rate in a vacuum?
a: Because the gravitational force is proportional to mass
Because heavy bodies have less air resistance
Because the feather is electrically charged
Because there is no gravity in a vacuum
116516.e: A body twice as heavy experiences twice the force, but also needs twice the force for the same acceleration. The mass cancels out, so the acceleration due to gravity is the same.
116516.m: Without air, all bodies fall at the same rate.

116517.q: Roughly what is the value of the gravitational constant G?
116517.e: The gravitational constant is very small: about 6.674·10^-11 m³ per kilogram and second squared. That is why you do not notice the attraction between everyday objects.
116517.m: The gravitational constant is a tiny number.

116518.q: What is the gravitational force between two masses of 1 kg each at a distance of 1 m?
116518.e: With F = G·1 kg·1 kg/(1 m)², the force equals exactly the numerical value of G. That is about 6.7·10^-11 newtons.
116518.m: Two one-kilogram weights attract each other almost imperceptibly.

116519.q: What distinguishes the gravitational constant G from the gravitational acceleration g?
a: G is the same everywhere, g depends on the celestial body
G is smaller on the Moon than on Earth
g is a constant of nature, G is not
116519.e: G is a universal constant of nature in the law of gravitation. The gravitational acceleration g results from the mass and radius of a particular celestial body.
116519.m: Big G is universal, small g depends on location.

116520.q: How can the Earth’s mass be calculated using G, g and the Earth’s radius R?
116520.e: At the Earth’s surface, g = G·M/R². Solving for M gives M = g·R²/G, which comes to about 6·10^24 kg.
116520.m: If you know G, you can calculate the Earth’s mass.

116521.q: What is special about G compared with other constants of nature?
a: It is only known relatively imprecisely
It only applies in the solar system
116521.e: Because gravity is very weak, G is hard to measure in the laboratory. It is known much less precisely than, for example, the speed of light or the elementary charge.
116521.m: The gravitational constant is one of the least precisely known constants of nature.

116522.q: Two lead balls of 100 kg each have their centres 0.5 m apart. Roughly what is their mutual attraction?
116522.e: With F = G·m1·m2/r², F = 6.67·10^-11 · 100 · 100 / 0.25 N. That gives about 2.7·10^-6 newtons, only a few millionths of a newton.
116522.m: Even heavy lead balls attract each other only very weakly.

116523.q: What is the SI unit of the gravitational constant?
116523.e: From G = F·r²/(m1·m2), the unit is N·m²/kg². With N = kg·m/s², this gives m³/(kg·s²).
116523.m: The unit of G follows directly from the law of gravitation.

116524.q: How strong is the gravity between two protons compared with their electrical repulsion?
116524.e: The electric force between two protons exceeds their gravity by about 36 orders of magnitude. Gravity only dominates with huge, electrically neutral masses.
116524.m: Gravity is the weakest of the fundamental forces.

116525.q: What does Kepler’s first law state?
a: Planets move in ellipses, with the Sun at one focus
Planets move in circles around the Earth
All planets have the same orbital period
The Sun is at the centre of a circular orbit
116525.e: Kepler realised that planetary orbits are ellipses. The Sun is not at the centre but at one of the two foci.
116525.m: Planetary orbits are ellipses with the Sun at a focus.

116526.q: Which relationship does Kepler’s third law describe?
a: Between a planet’s orbital period and the size of its orbit
Between a planet’s mass and brightness
Between the shape of the orbit and the planet’s colour
Between a planet’s rotation and temperature
116526.e: In 1619 Kepler found that the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. Planets further out therefore take much longer for one orbit.
116526.m: Kepler’s third law links orbital period and orbit size.

116527.q: A planet orbits the Sun with a semi-major axis of 4 AU. How long does one orbit take?
116527.e: According to Kepler’s third law, T² = a³ in years and AU. So T² = 4³ = 64 and T = 8 years.
116527.m: The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis.

116528.q: From the orbit of which planet did Kepler recognise that orbits are ellipses?
116528.e: The orbit of Mars differs relatively clearly from a circle. The precise position data did not fit any circular model, but they did fit an ellipse.
116528.m: The orbit of Mars revealed the elliptical shape to Kepler.

116529.q: In which year did Kepler publish his first two laws in the work “Astronomia nova”?
116529.e: “Astronomia nova” appeared in 1609. In it, Kepler explained the motion of the planets physically for the first time.
116529.m: Kepler published his first two laws in 1609.

116530.q: Which conservation law lies behind Kepler’s second law?
a: Conservation of momentum in a straight line
116530.e: The gravitational force always acts towards the Sun and therefore exerts no torque. Angular momentum is conserved, which corresponds to the law of equal areas.
116530.m: The law of equal areas is a consequence of the conservation of angular momentum.

116531.q: Mars has a semi-major axis of about 1.52 AU. Roughly how long is a Martian year?
116531.e: With T = a^1.5, this gives 1.52^1.5, so about 1.88 years. A Martian year therefore lasts almost two Earth years.
116531.m: Further out, planets need longer for one orbit.

116532.q: A comet has an orbital period of 27 years. What is its semi-major axis?
116532.e: From T² = a³ it follows that a³ = 27² = 729. Its cube root is 9, so 9 AU.
116532.m: Kepler’s third law lets you calculate the size of an orbit from the orbital period.

116533.q: Which quantity did Newton add to Kepler’s third law T² = 4π²·a³/(G·M)?
a: The mass of the central body
The mass of the planet alone
116533.e: Newton derived Kepler’s law from gravitation. This shows that the ratio T²/a³ depends on the mass of the central body.
116533.m: From orbital period and orbital radius you can determine the mass of the central body.

116534.q: By what factor is the escape velocity greater than the circular orbital speed at the same place?
116534.e: The circular orbital speed is √(GM/r), the escape velocity √(2GM/r). The ratio is therefore √2, about 1.41.
116534.m: The escape velocity is √2 times the circular orbital speed.

116535.q: Does the escape velocity depend on the mass of the flying body?
a: No, only on the mass and radius of the celestial body
116535.e: In the derivation, kinetic energy is set equal to binding energy. The body’s mass is on both sides and cancels out.
116535.m: The escape velocity is the same for a grain of sand and a rocket.

116536.q: Roughly what is the escape velocity at the Moon’s surface?
116536.e: The Moon has only just over 1 per cent of the Earth’s mass. With its mass and its radius of 1737 km, the result is about 2.4 km/s.
116536.m: It is much easier to get away from the Moon than from the Earth.

116537.q: Why does the Moon have practically no atmosphere?
a: Gas particles easily reach its low escape velocity
The Moon is too cold for gases
The Earth sucks the gases away
116537.e: Fast gas molecules can reach the Moon’s low escape velocity. Over a long time they escape into space, especially as the Moon has no magnetic field for protection.
116537.m: A low escape velocity lets gases escape.

116538.q: A planet has four times the Earth’s mass but the same radius. How does its escape velocity compare with the Earth’s?
116538.e: The escape velocity is proportional to the square root of M/R. With four times the mass and the same radius, this gives √4 = 2.
116538.m: The escape velocity grows with the square root of the mass.

116539.q: What is true of the escape velocity at the Schwarzschild radius of a black hole?
a: It equals the speed of light
It equals the speed of sound
It is half the speed of light
116539.e: The Schwarzschild radius is the radius at which the escape velocity reaches the speed of light. Not even light can escape from inside it.
116539.m: At the event horizon, the escape velocity equals the speed of light.

116540.q: To what radius would the Earth have to be squeezed to become a black hole?
116540.e: The Schwarzschild radius is r = 2GM/c². For the Earth’s mass, this gives about 8.9 millimetres.
116540.m: The Earth would have to become smaller than a marble to be a black hole.

116541.q: What is the first cosmic velocity for a circular orbit just above the Earth’s surface?
116541.e: For a circular orbit, gravity must provide exactly the centripetal force. With v = √(GM/R), you get about 7.9 km/s.
116541.m: For an orbit around the Earth you need about 7.9 km/s.

116542.q: Which simplified formula can be used to calculate the first cosmic velocity from g and the Earth’s radius R?
116542.e: At the surface, the weight m·g provides the centripetal force m·v²/R. From this, v² = g·R, using g = 9.81 m/s² and R = 6371 km.
116542.m: For a circular orbit close to the ground, v squared equals g times R.

116543.q: What is Newton’s thought experiment called that explains why a satellite falls around the Earth?
116543.e: Newton imagined a cannon on a high mountain. If the ball is fast enough, the Earth curves away beneath it as much as it falls, and it goes round the Earth.
116543.m: A satellite is constantly falling around the Earth.

116544.q: How long would one orbit on a circular path just above the Earth’s surface take without air resistance?
116544.e: The Earth’s circumference is about 40,000 km. Dividing it by the circular orbital speed close to the ground gives just over 5000 seconds, so about 84 minutes.
116544.m: An orbit of the Earth close to the ground would take about an hour and a half.

116545.q: How does the required circular orbital speed change with increasing height above the Earth?
a: It only becomes zero above 1000 km
116545.e: For circular orbits, v = √(GM/r). As the orbital radius grows, the speed becomes smaller, but the period becomes longer.
116545.m: High satellites fly more slowly than low ones.

116546.q: Why do rockets usually launch towards the east?
a: They make use of the Earth’s rotational speed
Gravity is weaker in the east
The wind always blows to the east
The Sun pulls them to the east
116546.e: The Earth turns from west to east. At the equator this already provides about 0.46 km/s, which the rocket then does not have to make up.

116547.q: Why can a satellite at a height of about 150 km not stay in its orbit for long?
a: The remaining air slows it down
It is too fast for an orbit
116547.e: At this height there is still thin air that slows the satellite down through friction. It loses height and burns up in the atmosphere after a short time.
116547.m: Low satellites are slowed down by the remaining atmosphere.

116548.q: Roughly how fast does the Moon move in its orbit around the Earth?
116548.e: The Moon is about 384,000 km away and takes just over 27 days for one orbit. This gives about 1.0 km/s.
116548.m: The Moon circles the Earth at about 1 km/s.

116549.q: What is an orbit called that has a period of one sidereal day and is inclined to the equator?
116549.e: A geosynchronous orbit has the same period as the Earth’s rotation. If it is inclined, the satellite traces a figure of eight in the sky instead of standing still.
116549.m: Every geostationary orbit is geosynchronous, but not the other way round.

116550.q: What exactly is the period of a geostationary satellite?
a: One sidereal day of about 23 h 56 min
116550.e: The satellite must turn as fast as the Earth does relative to the stars. This rotation takes one sidereal day, about 4 minutes shorter than a solar day.
116550.m: A geostationary satellite circles once per sidereal day.

116551.q: Why do geostationary satellites have to be exactly above the equator?
a: Only there does the orbital plane lie in the plane of the Earth’s rotation
Because there is no gravity there
Because there is no air there
Because the magnetic field is strongest there
116551.e: Every orbit goes around the centre of the Earth. An inclined orbit would make the satellite swing north and south every day.
116551.m: Geostationary only works above the equator.

116552.q: Roughly in which direction do satellite dishes point in Switzerland?
116552.e: Seen from Switzerland, television satellites are above the plane of the equator. Depending on the satellite, the dish points slightly south-east or south-west.

116553.q: Roughly how long does a radio signal take from the ground to a geostationary satellite and back to the ground?
116553.e: The distance is at least 2 times 35,786 km, so about 71,600 km. Divided by the speed of light of 300,000 km/s, this gives about 0.24 seconds.
116553.m: Signals via geostationary satellites have a noticeable delay.

116554.q: Roughly how fast does a geostationary satellite move in its orbit?
116554.e: The orbit’s circumference is 2π times 42,164 km, so about 265,000 km. Divided by one sidereal day of 86,164 s, this gives about 3.07 km/s.
116554.m: Geostationary satellites fly at about 3 km/s.

116555.q: Which writer suggested in 1945 using geostationary satellites for worldwide radio links?
116555.e: In an article, Arthur C. Clarke described a network of three satellites in geostationary orbit. That is why the orbit is sometimes called the Clarke orbit.
116555.m: Arthur C. Clarke thought up communication satellites ahead of time.

116556.q: Which regions can geostationary satellites not cover?
116556.e: From the poles, the satellites are below or only just above the horizon. At high latitudes, reception is therefore impossible or hardly possible.
116556.m: Above the poles you cannot see geostationary satellites.

116557.q: Which European organisation, of which Switzerland is also a member, operates the geostationary Meteosat weather satellites?
116557.e: EUMETSAT operates the Meteosat satellites, which constantly look down on Europe and Africa. Switzerland is one of the member states.
116557.m: Meteosat weather images come from geostationary satellites.

116558.q: What are the particularly weak tides at half moon called?
116558.e: At half moon, the Sun and the Moon are at right angles to each other as seen from the Earth. Their tidal effects partly cancel out, and the tidal range is small.
116558.m: At half moon, the tides are weak.

116559.q: Why is there also a tidal bulge on the side of the Earth facing away from the Moon?
a: There the Moon’s pull is weaker than at the Earth’s centre
There the Moon pushes the water away
116559.e: The tidal force is the difference in the Moon’s pull at different places. On the far side, the water lags behind the Earth, which is pulled more strongly.
116559.m: Tides arise from differences in gravitational pull.

116560.q: In which bay are the greatest tidal ranges in the world measured?
116560.e: In the Bay of Fundy in Canada, the tidal range can reach about 16 metres. The shape of the bay strengthens the tidal wave through resonance.
116560.m: The shape of a bay can greatly strengthen the tides.

116561.q: With which power of the distance does the tidal force decrease?
116561.e: The tidal force is the difference in gravity across the diameter of a body. Mathematically, it therefore falls off with 1/r³.
116561.m: Tidal forces fall with the third power of the distance.

116562.q: Roughly how large is the Sun’s tidal effect compared with the Moon’s?
116562.e: The Sun is much more massive but also much further away. Because of the dependence on 1/r³, its effect is only about 46 per cent of the Moon’s.
116562.m: The Moon influences the tides more strongly than the Sun.

116563.q: Why are there practically no visible tides on Lake Geneva?
a: The lake is too small for a measurable difference in force
Fresh water is not attracted by the Moon
The Rhône washes the high tide away
116563.e: Tides arise from differences in the Moon’s pull across a body of water. Over the length of a lake these differences are tiny, and the effects are at most in the millimetre range.
116563.m: Noticeable tides only occur in large seas.

116564.q: What is the minimum distance called below which a moon would be torn apart by tidal forces?
116564.e: If a moon comes too close to its planet, the tidal forces exceed its own gravity. Saturn’s rings lie mostly within this limit.
116564.m: Too close to the planet, tidal forces tear a moon apart.

116565.q: Why does the Moon always show us the same side?
a: Tidal forces have locked its rotation to its orbit
The Moon does not rotate at all
The Earth turns as fast as the Moon
The Sun holds it in place
116565.e: Friction from tidal deformation slowed down the Moon’s own rotation over a long time. Today one rotation takes exactly as long as one orbit.
116565.m: The Moon is tidally locked to the Earth.

116566.q: How strong is the Earth’s gravity at the height of the ISS, about 400 km, compared with the Earth’s surface?
116566.e: With g = GM/r² and r = 6771 km, the result is about 8.7 m/s², just under 90 per cent of 9.81 m/s². Gravity there is therefore almost as strong as on the ground.
116566.m: On the ISS, almost the full force of the Earth’s gravity acts.

116567.q: Why do astronauts float on the ISS?
a: The station and the people are in free fall together
There is no gravity in space
116567.e: The ISS and everything in it are constantly falling around the Earth with the same acceleration. That is why bodies do not press against each other, and weightlessness results.
116567.m: Weightlessness is a state of free fall.

116568.q: Roughly at what speed does the ISS fly at a height of about 400 km?
116568.e: For a circular orbit, v = √(GM/r) with r = 6771 km. That gives about 7.67 km/s, so over 27,000 km/h.
116568.m: The ISS flies around the Earth at over 27,000 km/h.

116569.q: How is the body mass of astronauts measured on the ISS?
a: With a spring oscillation and F = m·a
116569.e: Scales measure weight, which is missing in free fall. Instead, the person is accelerated by a spring or set oscillating, and the inertial mass is calculated from the motion.

116570.q: Roughly how long does weightlessness last per parabola on a parabolic flight?
116570.e: The aircraft flies a projectile parabola in which passengers and aircraft fall together. Each phase lasts about 20 seconds and is often repeated.
116570.m: Parabolic flights create short phases of weightlessness.

116571.q: Why does a candle flame burn in a ball shape in weightlessness?
a: Without buoyancy there is no convection
116571.e: On Earth, hot, light combustion gases rise and pull the flame upwards into a long shape. Without weight this buoyancy is missing, and the flame spreads out evenly.
116571.m: In weightlessness, hot gases have no buoyancy.

116572.q: Why is it more accurate, technically, to speak of microgravity rather than weightlessness on the ISS?
a: Because gravity there is a million times stronger
Because there are small black holes there
116572.e: Air friction, movements of the crew and the size of the station produce tiny accelerations. They are in the range of millionths of g.
116572.m: On the ISS there is microgravity.

116573.q: Why would you not be weightless at the top of a tower 400 km high?
a: Because it is not in free fall and you stand on it
Because the air is too thick there
116573.e: On a tower, almost the same gravity acts as on the ISS. But because the tower is connected to the Earth and holds you up, you feel your weight.
116573.m: Without free fall there is no weightlessness.

116574.q: How many Lagrange points are there in a system of two celestial bodies?
116574.e: Three points lie on the line joining the two bodies, and two more form equilateral triangles with them. They are called L1 to L5.

116575.q: At which Lagrange point of the Sun-Earth system is the James Webb Space Telescope located?
116575.e: L2 lies about 1.5 million km from the Earth on the side facing away from the Sun. There the telescope can keep the Sun, Earth and Moon behind its sunshield at the same time.
116575.m: The James Webb Telescope works at point L2.

116576.q: Which Lagrange point is particularly suitable for constant observation of the Sun?
116576.e: L1 lies between the Earth and the Sun and offers a clear view of the Sun. The solar observatory SOHO, for example, works there.
116576.m: From point L1 you can see the Sun without interruption.

116577.q: Which Lagrange points are stable if the mass ratio is large enough?
116577.e: L1, L2 and L3 are unstable, and satellites there have to correct their orbits regularly. L4 and L5 are stable if the main body is about 25 times more massive than the second.
116577.m: Only L4 and L5 hold bodies in place by themselves.

116578.q: What are the asteroids called that gather at Jupiter’s L4 and L5 points?
116578.e: Thousands of asteroids stay at the Lagrange points ahead of and behind Jupiter. They were named after heroes of the Trojan War.
116578.m: Jupiter’s Trojans circle at its Lagrange points.

116579.q: What geometric figure do L4 and L5 each form with the two main bodies?
116579.e: L4 runs 60 degrees ahead of the smaller body, and L5 follows it by 60 degrees. With the two main bodies, each forms an equilateral triangle.
116579.m: L4 and L5 lie at the tips of equilateral triangles.

116580.q: Where is the Lagrange point L3 in the Sun-Earth system?
a: Behind the Sun on the opposite side from the Earth
Between the Earth and the Moon
116580.e: L3 lies on the connecting line, but on the side of the Sun opposite the Earth. It can never be seen directly from the Earth.

116581.q: What balance exists at a Lagrange point in the rotating frame?
a: Gravitational forces and centrifugal force cancel out
Electric and magnetic forces cancel out
116581.e: A small body can move along there with the same period as the second main body. In the rotating frame of reference, the resultant force is zero.
116581.m: At Lagrange points, the forces cancel out in the rotating frame.

116582.q: In which year did Henry Cavendish publish the results of his famous gravitation experiment?
116582.e: Cavendish carried out his measurements in 1797 and 1798 and published them in 1798. It was the first measurement of gravity between bodies in a laboratory.
116582.m: Cavendish measured gravity in the laboratory in 1798.

116583.q: Which measuring instrument did Cavendish use?
116583.e: Two small lead balls hung on a rod from a thin wire. Large lead balls attracted them, and the tiny twist of the wire showed the force.

116584.q: Which quantity did Cavendish originally want to determine with his experiment?
a: The average density of the Earth
116584.e: Cavendish was interested in the density of the Earth. The gravitational constant could later also be calculated from his data.
116584.m: Cavendish actually wanted to weigh the Earth.

116585.q: Roughly what value for the Earth’s average density did Cavendish obtain?
116585.e: Cavendish arrived at about 5.45 g per cm³. Today’s value of about 5.51 g per cm³ is only about 1 per cent higher.
116585.m: On average, the Earth is more than five times denser than water.

116586.q: Why did Cavendish watch the torsion balance from outside the room through a telescope?
a: So that air currents and body heat would not disturb the measurement
Because the room was under water
116586.e: The gravitational forces between the balls were tiny. Even small air movements caused by temperature differences would have spoiled the measurement.
116586.m: Small forces require a measurement free from disturbance.

116587.q: Why was the Cavendish experiment so difficult to carry out?
a: The attraction between the balls is tiny
Lead was hardly available at the time
There were no accurate clocks yet
116587.e: The gravitational force between balls in the laboratory is millions of times smaller than their weight. Cavendish therefore needed an extremely sensitive torsion balance, originally built by John Michell.
116587.m: Gravity between everyday objects is tiny.

116588.q: What were the balls in the Cavendish experiment made of?
116588.e: Lead has a high density, so a lot of mass fits into a small space. The large balls each weighed about 158 kg.
116588.m: Heavy lead balls made the tiny attraction measurable.

116589.q: Which chemical element had Henry Cavendish already described as a separate substance in 1766?
116589.e: Cavendish studied the “inflammable air” produced when metals react with acids. He recognised it as a separate substance, hydrogen.

116590.q: What is the unit of gravitational field strength?
116590.e: Field strength gives the force per mass. The unit N/kg is equivalent to m/s².
116590.m: Gravitational field strength is measured in newtons per kilogram.

116591.q: Roughly what is the gravitational acceleration at the Moon’s surface?
116591.e: With a lunar mass of 7.34·10^22 kg and a radius of 1737 km, g = GM/R² gives about 1.62 m/s². That is about one sixth of the Earth’s value.
116591.m: On the Moon you weigh about one sixth.

116592.q: At what height above the Earth’s surface is the field strength only one ninth of its value at the ground?
a: At a height of two Earth radii
At a height of one Earth radius
At a height of three Earth radii
At a height of nine Earth radii
116592.e: The field strength falls with 1/r², measured from the centre of the Earth. One ninth means r = 3R, so a height of 2R above the surface.
116592.m: For gravity, heights must be measured from the centre of the Earth.

116593.q: What is the gravitational field strength inside a hollow spherical shell of even thickness?
a: The same as at the surface
116593.e: According to Newton’s shell theorem, the pulls of all parts of the shell cancel each other out exactly inside it. A body inside feels no force from the shell.
116593.m: Inside a hollow sphere, gravity cancels out.

116594.q: Why is the gravitational acceleration at the poles slightly greater than at the equator?
a: The Earth is flattened there and there is no centrifugal force
The poles are closer to the Sun
116594.e: At the poles you are closer to the centre of the Earth, and the Earth’s rotation produces no centrifugal force there. That is why g is about 9.83 instead of about 9.78 m/s².
116594.m: At the poles, gravity is slightly stronger.

116595.q: How do the field lines run in the gravitational field of a sphere?
116595.e: The field lines show the direction of the force on a test mass. Because gravity always attracts, they run radially towards the centre of the sphere.
116595.m: Gravitational field lines point towards the centre of the mass.

116596.q: What is the surface of equal gravitational potential called that roughly corresponds to mean sea level?
116596.e: The geoid is an equipotential surface of the Earth’s gravitational field. National surveys such as swisstopo’s base their height data on such a model.
116596.m: The geoid describes the shape of the Earth’s gravitational field.

116597.q: What is the gravitational potential at a distance r from a point mass M if it is zero at infinity?
116597.e: The potential gives the potential energy per mass. Because work is needed to get to infinity, it is negative everywhere and equals -GM/r.
116597.m: Gravitational potential is negative and rises towards zero further out.

116598.q: What is the eccentricity of a circular orbit?
116598.e: Eccentricity measures how far an orbit differs from a circle. A circle has an eccentricity of 0, and ellipses lie between 0 and 1.
116598.m: A circle is an ellipse with an eccentricity of zero.

116599.q: Roughly what is the eccentricity of the Earth’s orbit?
116599.e: The Earth’s orbit is almost a circle, with an eccentricity of about 0.0167. Its distance from the Sun therefore varies by only just over 3 per cent.
116599.m: The Earth’s orbit is almost circular.

116600.q: How do you calculate a planet’s closest distance to the Sun from the semi-major axis a and eccentricity e?
116600.e: The focus lies a·e away from the centre of the ellipse. The shortest distance is therefore a minus a·e, which is a·(1-e).
116600.m: The perihelion lies at a distance of a times one minus e.

116601.q: Which planet in the solar system has the greatest orbital eccentricity?
116601.e: Mercury has an eccentricity of about 0.21. Its distance from the Sun therefore varies much more than that of the other planets.
116601.m: Mercury has the most elliptical planetary orbit.

116602.q: What shape of path does a body have that is moving at exactly escape velocity?
116602.e: At exactly escape velocity, the total energy is zero and the path is a parabola with an eccentricity of 1. At higher speed it becomes a hyperbola.
116602.m: At exactly escape velocity, a body flies along a parabola.

116603.q: Halley’s Comet has an orbital period of about 76 years. Roughly what is its semi-major axis?
116603.e: From a³ = T² it follows that a³ = 76² = 5776. The cube root gives about 17.9 AU.
116603.m: Comets such as Halley’s travel on very elongated ellipses.

116604.q: Which quantity alone determines the period of a body on an elliptical orbit around the same central body?
116604.e: According to Kepler’s third law, the period depends only on the semi-major axis. A highly eccentric ellipse and a circle with the same a have the same period.
116604.m: The period depends only on the semi-major axis.

116605.q: Which auxin occurs most commonly in plants naturally?
116605.e: Indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) is the most important natural auxin. Gibberellic acid, zeatin and abscisic acid belong to other groups of hormones.
116605.m: The most important natural auxin is indole-3-acetic acid.

116606.q: Where is auxin mainly produced in a plant?
a: In shoot tips and young leaves
In the bark of the trunk
116606.e: Auxin is produced mainly in growing tissues at the shoot tip and in young leaves. From there it is transported downwards.
116606.m: Auxin is produced mainly in the shoot tips.

116607.q: Why does a seedling lit from one side bend towards the light?
a: Auxin moves to the shaded side and promotes elongation there
Auxin moves to the lit side and promotes elongation there
Light destroys the cell walls on the shaded side
Chlorophyll pulls the shoot tip towards the light
116607.e: When light comes from one side, auxin is moved to the shaded side. There the cells elongate more, so the shoot bends towards the light.
116607.m: In phototropism, auxin stretches the shaded side of the shoot.

116608.q: Which researchers showed in 1880, using grass seedlings, that the tip senses the light stimulus?
116608.e: Charles Darwin and his son Francis covered the tips of coleoptiles and described the experiments in 1880 in “The Power of Movement in Plants”. Without a lit tip, the bending did not happen.
116608.m: The Darwins found that the seedling tip senses the light.

116609.q: Seedling tips are placed on small agar blocks, and the blocks are then put on decapitated seedlings. These grow again. What does this prove?
a: A chemical substance from the tip triggers growth
Agar naturally contains a plant hormone
Seedlings without tips always grow faster
116609.e: The substance from the tip had passed into the agar and kept working there. In this way Frits Went demonstrated auxin in the 1920s.
116609.m: Agar experiments proved that auxin is a chemical growth substance.

116610.q: Why are cuttings in horticulture often dipped in a powder containing synthetic auxin?
116610.e: Auxins such as indole-3-butyric acid stimulate the formation of adventitious roots at the cut. That is why rooting powders contain such substances.
116610.m: Rooting powder contains auxin so that cuttings form roots faster.

116611.q: Which synthetic auxin is used as a herbicide against broadleaf weeds in cereal crops?
116611.e: 2,4-D acts like an overdose of auxin and makes broadleaf plants grow uncontrollably until they die. Grasses such as cereals are less sensitive.
116611.m: The herbicide 2,4-D kills weeds with an overdose of auxin action.

116612.q: How is auxin usually transported in the plant?
a: In one direction from cell to cell, from the tip downwards
Upwards with the water in the xylem
Through the air from leaf to leaf
Not at all, it stays where it is made
116612.e: Auxin is transported in a polar way: transport proteins, the PIN proteins, sit on only one side of the cells and pass it on in one direction.
116612.m: Auxin moves in one direction, from the shoot tip downwards.

116613.q: According to the acid growth theory, how does auxin promote cell elongation?
a: Protons are pumped into the cell wall and loosen it
The cell wall is strengthened with extra cellulose
The nucleus divides several times in quick succession
The vacuole releases water into the surroundings
116613.e: Auxin activates proton pumps in the cell membrane, and the cell wall becomes acidic. This activates enzymes such as expansins, which loosen the wall, so turgor can stretch the cell.
116613.m: According to the acid growth theory, an acidified cell wall loosens its structure for elongation.

116614.q: In which crop did the fungal disease “bakanae” lead to the discovery of gibberellins?
116614.e: The fungus Gibberella fujikuroi attacked rice plants in Japan and greatly changed their growth. Japanese researchers isolated the active substance from it, gibberellin.
116614.m: Gibberellins were discovered through a fungal disease of rice.

116615.q: Which symptom do rice plants suffering from “bakanae” disease show?
116615.e: “Bakanae” means roughly “foolish seedling” in Japanese. The infected plants grow too tall, fall over and give little yield.
116615.m: Too much gibberellin makes plants grow excessively tall.

116616.q: Which enzyme does the aleurone layer of a germinating barley grain produce in response to a gibberellin signal?
116616.e: The embryo sends gibberellins to the aleurone layer. This produces alpha-amylase, which breaks down the starch in the endosperm into sugar and feeds the embryo.
116616.m: Gibberellins make the germinating grain produce a starch-digesting enzyme.

116617.q: What are the short stems of many Green Revolution wheat varieties based on?
a: Too much auxin in the stem
A lack of phytochrome in the shoot
116617.e: The so-called Rht genes change proteins in the gibberellin signalling pathway, so the stems respond less to the hormone. Short stems do not bend over under heavy ears.
116617.m: The short stems of modern wheat varieties respond more weakly to gibberellins.

116618.q: How do plants grow that can hardly make any gibberellins themselves?
116618.e: Gibberellins promote stem elongation. Without the hormone, plants stay small. Mendel's short peas also had a defect in gibberellin production.

116619.q: Which group of plant hormones mainly promotes stem elongation and germination?
116619.e: Gibberellins make shoots grow longer and break seed dormancy. Abscisic acid, by contrast, has an inhibiting effect, and ethylene promotes fruit ripening.
116619.m: Gibberellins promote stem elongation and germination.

116620.q: Which process do gibberellins trigger in rosette plants such as lettuce?
a: Bolting of a long flower stalk
Rolling up of the leaves in heat
116620.e: Rosette plants have compressed shoots. Gibberellins cause the internodes to stretch strongly, so the plant “bolts” and forms a flower stalk.
116620.m: Gibberellins make rosette plants shoot up.

116621.q: Why are seedless table grapes often sprayed with gibberellic acid during growing?
a: So that the berries become larger
So that the berries form seeds
So that the grapes fall off earlier
So that the skin becomes darker
116621.e: In seedless varieties, gibberellic acid promotes the growth of the berries and loosens the bunch. This produces larger fruit.
116621.m: Gibberellic acid makes the berries of seedless grapes bigger.

116622.q: How do stem shorteners such as chlormequat work in cereal growing?
a: They inhibit the production of gibberellins
They promote the production of gibberellins
They block the uptake of nitrogen
116622.e: Chlormequat inhibits enzymes of gibberellin synthesis. The stems stay shorter and sturdier, so the crop falls over less.
116622.m: Stem shorteners slow gibberellin production and make cereals sturdier.

116623.q: Where are cytokinins mainly produced in the plant?
116623.e: Cytokinins are produced mainly in the root tips and travel with the xylem sap into the shoot.
116623.m: Cytokinins are produced mainly in the root tips.

116624.q: Which group of substances do cytokinins such as zeatin, obtained from maize, belong to?
116624.e: Cytokinins are plant hormones that control cell division and growth. The natural cytokinin zeatin was isolated from unripe maize kernels and named after Zea mays.

116625.q: Which process do cytokinins promote, as their name also suggests?
116625.e: The name comes from cytokinesis, the division of the cytoplasm. Together with auxin, cytokinins stimulate cell division.

116626.q: What are cytokinins used for in the laboratory when propagating plants from tissue cultures?
a: To make new shoots grow from clumps of cells
To make the plants dry out faster
116626.e: From an undifferentiated clump of cells, the callus, shoots form with a lot of cytokinin and little auxin. A lot of auxin, on the other hand, promotes roots.
116626.m: Cytokinins make shoots form in tissue culture.

116627.q: What can be seen on a cut leaf that is treated with cytokinin?
a: It rolls up into a spiral
116627.e: Cytokinins delay the breakdown of chlorophyll and proteins. Treated areas of the leaf stay green and even attract nutrients.
116627.m: Cytokinins keep leaves green for longer.

116628.q: Which bacterium causes crown galls by transferring genes for making auxin and cytokinin into the plant?
116628.e: Agrobacterium tumefaciens inserts part of its Ti plasmid into the plant's genome. The plant cells then produce hormones uncontrollably and grow into a gall.
116628.m: Agrobacterium makes plants form galls through foreign hormone genes.

116629.q: From which nucleobase are natural cytokinins chemically derived?
116629.e: Cytokinins are adenine derivatives with a side chain on the nitrogen atom N6. Zeatin, for example, carries an isoprenoid side chain.
116629.m: Cytokinins are chemically modified adenine molecules.

116630.q: How do cytokinins affect dormant side buds of a shoot?
a: They make them dry out and fall off
116630.e: Cytokinins counteract the inhibiting effect of the shoot tip. Applied to side buds, they make them sprout.
116630.m: Cytokinins wake up dormant side buds.

116631.q: How do the stomata react when the level of abscisic acid in the leaf rises during drought?
116631.e: Abscisic acid makes the stomata close. This way the plant loses less water through transpiration when water is short.
116631.m: Abscisic acid closes the stomata in drought.

116632.q: What happens in the guard cells when abscisic acid acts?
a: Potassium ions and water flow out and turgor falls
Sugar is made and water flows in
The cell walls thicken with lignin
The chloroplasts move to the edge of the cell
116632.e: Abscisic acid opens ion channels, and potassium and chloride ions leave the guard cells. Water follows by osmosis, the turgor falls and the pore closes.
116632.m: Without turgor, the guard cells go slack and the pore closes.

116633.q: What happens to seeds that cannot make abscisic acid?
a: They germinate while still on the parent plant
116633.e: Abscisic acid keeps seeds dormant. Without it, seeds germinate too early, for example maize kernels still on the cob. This is called vivipary.
116633.m: Abscisic acid stops seeds from germinating too early.

116634.q: From which process does the name “abscisic acid” come?
a: From the shedding of plant organs
116634.e: The substance was studied in the 1960s in connection with the shedding of cotton fruits (abscission); Latin abscidere means “to cut off”. Today we know it plays only a minor role in this.
116634.m: The name abscisic acid recalls the shedding of plant parts.

116635.q: Which group of substances does abscisic acid belong to?
116635.e: Abscisic acid is a plant hormone. Even in small amounts it acts as a signal, for example for closing the stomata or for seed dormancy.
116635.m: Abscisic acid is a plant hormone.

116636.q: Why is abscisic acid often called a “stress hormone”?
a: Its level rises sharply in drought, cold or salt
It is only made when insects cause injuries
It makes the plant flower faster under stress
