a: Pump water up when there is surplus electricity, run it through turbines when needed
Evaporate water and drive turbines with steam
Let river water flow through without storage
116969.e: Surplus electricity pumps water into an upper reservoir. When electricity is needed, it flows back through turbines into the lower reservoir.
116969.m: A pumped storage plant stores electrical energy as the potential energy of water.

116970.q: How much energy is theoretically contained in 1 m³ of water (1000 kg) falling 600 m (with g = 9.81 m/s²)?
116970.e: E = 1000 · 9.81 · 600 J = 5,886,000 J. Divided by 3,600,000 J per kWh, this gives about 1.64 kWh.
116970.m: Pumped storage needs large amounts of water and large height differences.

116971.q: The pumps have an efficiency of 88 %, turbine operation 90 %. What is the overall efficiency of the storage cycle?
116971.e: The efficiencies are multiplied: 0.88 · 0.9 = 0.792, so about 79 %.
116971.m: Pumped storage only gives back part of the energy stored.

116972.q: How much energy do 1 million m³ of water pumped up by 500 m theoretically store (with g = 9.81 m/s²)?
116972.e: m = 10⁹ kg. E = 10⁹ · 9.81 · 500 J ≈ 4.9 · 10¹² J. Divided by 3.6 · 10⁶ J per kWh, this gives about 1.36 million kWh.
116972.m: Pumped storage can store energy in the gigawatt hour range.

116973.q: 100 MWh are used for pumping, and the overall efficiency is 80 %. How much energy is lost?
116973.e: 0.8 · 100 MWh = 80 MWh goes back into the grid. The difference of 20 MWh is lost, mainly as heat.
116973.m: The losses are the energy supplied minus the energy recovered.

116974.q: Roughly how much water per second does a power station need for 100 MW with a 400 m head and 90 % efficiency (using g = 9.81 m/s²)?
116974.e: From P = η · ρ · g · h · Q it follows that Q = 10⁸ W / (0.9 · 1000 · 9.81 · 400) ≈ 28.3 m³/s.
116974.m: The output of a hydroelectric power station depends on the head and the flow rate.

a: A machine that pumps or generates electricity depending on its direction of rotation
A pump that only extracts groundwater
A turbine driven by the wind
116975.e: In many pumped storage stations the same machine works as a pump in one direction of rotation and as a turbine in the other. This saves space and money.
116975.m: A pump turbine can pump water uphill and generate electricity.

116976.q: A pumped storage station buys electricity for 5 centimes per kWh and sells it for 12 centimes per kWh, at 80 % efficiency. How much is left over per 100 kWh bought?
116976.e: Buying: 100 kWh · 5 centimes = 5 francs. Selling: 80 kWh · 12 centimes = 9.60 francs. That leaves 4.60 francs.
116976.m: Pumped storage pays off when the price difference makes up for the losses.

116977.q: Which energy company is the main shareholder of Kraftwerke Linth-Limmern?
116977.e: Kraftwerke Linth-Limmern AG is mostly owned by Axpo; the canton of Glarus holds a minority stake.
116977.m: Kraftwerke Linth-Limmern is mostly owned by Axpo.

116978.q: Which lake serves as the upper reservoir of the Limmern pumped storage station?
116978.e: Water is pumped from the Limmernsee up into the higher Muttsee. When electricity is needed, it flows back down.
116978.m: The Muttsee is the upper reservoir of Limmern.

116979.q: Roughly how big is the difference in height between the Limmernsee and the Muttsee?
116979.e: According to the operator Axpo, the Muttsee lies just over 600 m higher than the Limmernsee.
116979.m: There are just over 600 metres of height between the Muttsee and the Limmernsee.

116980.q: Roughly how long is the dam at the Muttsee?
116980.e: The crest of the Muttsee dam is 1054 m long. According to Axpo, it is the longest dam in Switzerland.
116980.m: The Muttsee dam is over a kilometre long.

116981.q: How many pump turbines of 250 MW each are in the machine cavern at Limmern?
116981.e: Four machine sets stand in a cavern about 150 m long deep inside the mountain. Each machine can pump or generate electricity.
116981.m: Four large pump turbines work at Limmern.

116982.q: Roughly how much did it cost to build the Limmern pumped storage station?
116982.e: According to Axpo, the costs were about 2.1 billion francs, with a construction period of about seven years.
116982.m: Limmern is one of the most expensive power station projects in Switzerland.

116983.q: Roughly how much water per second is needed to generate 500 MW with a 600 m head and 90 % efficiency (using g = 9.81 m/s²)?
116983.m: Large outputs need an enormous flow of water, even with a high head.

116984.q: The Muttsee holds about 23 million m³. How much energy would it theoretically correspond to if this amount flowed 600 m down (using g = 9.81 m/s²)?
116984.e: E = 23 · 10⁹ kg · 9.81 m/s² · 600 m ≈ 1.35 · 10¹⁴ J. Divided by 3.6 · 10¹² J per GWh, that gives about 38 GWh.
116984.m: A large mountain lake theoretically stores energy in the range of dozens of gigawatt hours.

116985.e: 1 eV is the energy a particle with one elementary charge gains when it passes through 1 V: 1.602 · 10⁻¹⁹ C · 1 V.
116985.m: An electronvolt is a tiny amount of energy for single particles.

116986.q: An electron passes through a voltage of 5000 V. How much energy does it gain?
116986.e: A particle with one elementary charge gains 1 eV per volt. At 5000 V that is 5000 eV = 5 keV.
116986.m: An electron gains one electronvolt for every volt it passes through.

116987.q: An alpha particle (charge 2e) passes through 1000 V. How much energy does it gain?
116987.m: The energy gained in eV is the charge number times the voltage.

116988.m: Mega means one million, so one million electronvolts.

116989.q: What energy per beam have protons reached in the LHC at CERN near Geneva since 2022 (as of 2025)?
116989.e: In the third run, protons are accelerated to 6.8 TeV. In head-on collisions this gives 13.6 TeV.
116989.m: The LHC at CERN accelerates protons to teraelectronvolt energies.

116990.q: Roughly how large is the rest energy of a proton?
116990.e: According to E = m · c², the proton mass of 1.673 · 10⁻²⁷ kg corresponds to an energy of about 938 MeV, just under 1 GeV.
116990.m: A proton has a rest energy of just under one gigaelectronvolt.

116991.q: Roughly how large is the rest energy of an electron?
116991.e: According to E = m · c², the electron mass of 9.11 · 10⁻³¹ kg corresponds to an energy of about 511 keV.
116991.m: The rest energy of the electron is about half an MeV.

116993.q: What does the gravimetric energy density of an energy source tell you?
116993.e: Gravimetric energy density measures how much energy is contained in one kilogram, for example in kWh/kg or MJ/kg. Volumetric energy density refers to the volume.
116993.m: Energy density tells you how much energy is contained in a mass or a volume.

116994.q: Which energy source has the most energy per kilogram?
116994.e: Hydrogen has a calorific value of about 120 MJ/kg, almost three times as much as petrol with about 42 MJ/kg. Batteries store much less per kilogram.
116994.m: Hydrogen has the highest energy density per mass.

116995.q: A battery weighs 500 kg and has an energy density of 0.2 kWh/kg. How much energy does it store?
116995.m: Stored energy is mass times energy density.

116996.q: A tank holds 40 l of petrol with 8.8 kWh per litre. How much chemical energy is that?
116996.m: Petrol stores a lot of energy in a small volume.

116997.q: How many kilograms of water must be pumped up 500 m to store 1 kWh (using g = 9.81 m/s²)?
116997.m: The potential energy of water has a very low energy density.

116998.q: A vehicle battery stores 60 kWh and weighs 400 kg. What is its energy density?
116998.e: Energy density = energy / mass = 60 kWh / 400 kg = 0.15 kWh/kg.
116998.m: You get the energy density by dividing the energy by the mass.

116999.q: Why is hydrogen strongly compressed in vehicle tanks?
a: It has a low energy density per volume
116999.e: As a gas at normal pressure, hydrogen takes up a lot of space. That is why it is usually stored at 700 bar in vehicles.
116999.m: Hydrogen is rich in energy per mass but poor in energy per volume.

117000.q: A house needs 20,000 kWh of heat per year, and wood supplies about 4 kWh per kg. How much wood is needed without losses?
117000.e: m = 20,000 kWh / 4 kWh/kg = 5000 kg, so about 5 tonnes.
117000.m: The fuel mass needed is the energy demand divided by the energy density.

117001.q: What is the ionisation energy of a hydrogen atom in its ground state?
117001.e: To remove the electron completely from the ground state of the hydrogen atom takes 13.6 eV. This follows from the Bohr model of the atom and agrees with measurements.
117001.m: Atomic binding energies are in the range of a few electronvolts.

117002.q: A cyclist pedals at a constant 200 W for one hour. How much work does he do?

117003.q: Which of the following elements is one of the plant's macronutrients?
117003.e: Plants need potassium in large amounts, so it counts as a macronutrient. The plant needs boron, zinc and molybdenum only in traces.
117003.m: Potassium is a macronutrient for plants.

117004.q: In which form do plant roots take up potassium from the soil solution?
117004.e: Roots take up nutrients as dissolved ions, so potassium is taken up as a singly charged positive cation. The K2O figure on fertiliser bags is only a figure used for calculation.
117004.m: Plants take up potassium as a dissolved cation.

117005.q: What is the main job of potassium in the plant?
a: It controls the water balance and the stomata
It is the central atom of chlorophyll
It is a building block of DNA
It forms the framework of the cell wall
117005.e: Potassium ions regulate the osmotic pressure in the cells and so the opening and closing of the stomata. Plants well supplied with potassium are therefore less vulnerable to drought.
117005.m: Potassium regulates the plant's water balance.

117006.q: Which element sits as the central atom in the chlorophyll molecule?
117006.e: A magnesium ion is bound at the centre of the ring-shaped chlorophyll molecule. Without magnesium, the plant cannot make chlorophyll.
117006.m: Magnesium is the central atom of chlorophyll.

117007.q: For which amino acids does the plant need the macronutrient sulphur?
117007.e: Sulphur is part of the amino acids cysteine and methionine and therefore of many proteins. Rapeseed and cabbage have a particularly high need for sulphur.
117007.m: Sulphur is found in the amino acids cysteine and methionine.

117008.q: Which macronutrient is especially important for firm cell walls?
117008.e: Calcium strengthens cell walls and membranes. Without it, fruits and young tissues become soft and easily damaged.
117008.m: Calcium strengthens the plant's cell walls.

117009.q: What do the three numbers on a compound fertiliser labelled “NPK 15-15-15” indicate?
a: The percentages of nitrogen, phosphate and potash
The grams per square metre for three years
The solubility in three soil types
117009.e: The numbers give the percentages by mass: nitrogen as N, phosphate as P2O5 and potash as K2O. So a 100 kg bag contains 15 kg of each of these nutrients.
117009.m: The numbers on NPK fertiliser give nutrient contents in per cent.

117010.q: Which macronutrient do most crops need in the largest amount?
117010.e: Nitrogen is part of all amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids and chlorophyll. That is why it is the most important nutrient from the soil in terms of quantity.
117010.m: Nitrogen is the most important nutrient for plant growth.

117011.q: Which three main elements of biomass does the plant get mainly from air and water rather than from soil minerals?
117011.e: Carbon comes from CO2 in the air, hydrogen and oxygen from water and CO2. Together they make up over 90 per cent of the dry mass.
117011.m: A plant builds most of its mass from air and water.

117012.q: Which of these elements is a micronutrient for plants?
117012.e: Iron is needed only in small amounts but is essential, for example for enzymes of respiration and photosynthesis. Potassium, calcium and magnesium are macronutrients.

117013.q: How do micronutrients mainly differ from macronutrients?
a: Only in being taken up through the leaves
In occurring only in artificial fertiliser
117013.e: The plant needs micronutrients only in traces, macronutrients in much larger amounts. Both are essential: if one is missing, the plant cannot complete its life cycle.
117013.m: Micronutrients are just as vital but are needed only in traces.

117014.q: Why can iron deficiency be recognised by yellow leaves with green veins?
a: Without iron, too little chlorophyll is made
Iron makes the leaf veins grow
117014.e: Iron is not part of chlorophyll, but it is needed to make it. If it is missing, the young leaves turn yellow between the veins (chlorosis).
117014.m: Iron deficiency leads to yellow leaves.

117015.q: Why can too much of a micronutrient harm a plant?
a: Many micronutrients are toxic in larger amounts
It makes the plant grow too big
117015.e: Trace elements such as boron or copper are needed in small amounts but are toxic in larger ones. There is often only a narrow range between deficiency and excess.
117015.m: With trace elements, too much is harmful too.

117016.q: What is the best way to find out whether a plant lacks a micronutrient?
a: With a soil or leaf analysis
117016.e: Deficiency symptoms often look similar. An analysis of the soil or leaves in a laboratory shows which nutrient is actually missing.
117016.m: A soil or leaf analysis shows nutrient deficiency.

117017.q: Where does the oxygen released by plants in photosynthesis come from?
117017.e: In the light reactions, water is split, releasing oxygen. The carbon from CO2, on the other hand, is built into sugar.
117017.m: The oxygen from photosynthesis comes from water.

117018.q: Why are micronutrients also called trace elements?
a: The plant needs them only in traces
They leave traces in the soil
They only occur in traces left by animals
They are only found on paths
117018.e: The plant needs only tiny amounts of micronutrients, often a few grams per hectare per year. Even so, they are essential.
117018.m: Plants need trace elements only in tiny amounts.

117019.q: Which metal has long been sprayed in vineyards against fungal diseases and can build up in the soil?
117019.e: Copper products protect vines from downy mildew, even in organic farming. Copper is a micronutrient, but it builds up in the soil, where in large amounts it harms soil organisms.
117019.m: Copper is both a trace element and a plant protection product.

117020.q: Which chemist made the law of the minimum well known in the 19th century?
117020.e: Justus von Liebig spread the law in his writings on agricultural chemistry. That is why it is often called Liebig's law of the minimum.
117020.m: Liebig made the law of the minimum well known.

117021.q: What does the law of the minimum state?
a: The most plentiful nutrient determines the yield
More fertiliser always means a bigger yield
117021.e: Growth depends on the factor that is in shortest supply compared with what is needed. A surplus of other nutrients cannot make up for this shortage.
117021.m: The factor in shortest supply limits growth.

117022.q: Which ecological law extends the law of the minimum by saying that too much of a factor also limits growth?
117022.e: At the start of the 20th century, Victor Shelford described how every environmental factor has a range of tolerance with a minimum and a maximum. Too much fertiliser can therefore do as much harm as too little.
117022.m: A surplus can also limit growth.

117023.q: In Liebig's barrel, what does the shortest stave represent?
117023.e: The water in the barrel can only rise as high as the shortest stave. In the same way, the yield can only be as high as the scarcest factor allows.
117023.m: The shortest stave of Liebig's barrel shows the limiting factor.

117024.q: A soil contains too little phosphorus but enough nitrogen. According to the law of the minimum, what does extra nitrogen fertiliser achieve?
a: Making up for the phosphorus shortage
Faster root growth through more phosphorus
117024.e: As long as phosphorus is the limiting factor, the yield stays limited by it. Extra nitrogen is not used and may even be washed out.
117024.m: Fertilising only pays off with the nutrient in shortest supply.

117025.q: Why does each further dose of fertiliser usually bring a smaller and smaller extra yield?
a: Fertiliser becomes more toxic over time
Plants can only take up fertiliser in spring
117025.e: Once one nutrient is available in sufficient amounts, another factor such as water, light or a different nutrient becomes scarce. The yield then rises more and more slowly.
117025.m: More fertiliser only pays off up to a limit.

117026.q: Apart from nutrients, which factors can also be in shortest supply?
117026.e: The law of the minimum can be extended to all growth factors. In drought, cold or lack of light, more fertiliser brings no benefit either.
117026.m: Light, water and warmth can also limit growth.

117027.q: Which nutrient is the limiting factor for algal growth in many Swiss lakes?
117027.e: In lakes, phosphorus is often the scarcest nutrient, so extra phosphorus input leads to algal blooms. That is why Switzerland banned phosphates in laundry detergents in 1986.
117027.m: In many lakes, phosphorus limits algal growth.

117028.q: Which enzyme converts atmospheric nitrogen during biological nitrogen fixation?
117028.e: Nitrogenase breaks the stable N2 bond and reduces the nitrogen. Only certain bacteria and archaea have this enzyme.
117028.m: Nitrogenase fixes nitrogen from the air.

117029.q: Which compound is formed directly from N2 in biological nitrogen fixation?
117029.e: Nitrogenase reduces N2 to ammonia (NH3). This is then quickly built into amino acids.

117030.q: Why can plants not use the nitrogen in the air themselves, even though air is about 78 per cent nitrogen?
a: Because the triple bond in the N2 molecule is very stable
Because nitrogen in the air is poisonous
Because nitrogen does not fit through stomata
Because atmospheric nitrogen only occurs at night
117030.e: The two nitrogen atoms are joined by a very high-energy triple bond. Only certain microorganisms have an enzyme that can break it under normal conditions.
117030.m: The triple bond makes atmospheric nitrogen so unreactive.

117031.q: Which genus of free-living soil bacteria fixes atmospheric nitrogen without a symbiosis with a plant?
117031.e: Azotobacter lives freely in well-aerated soils and fixes nitrogen for its own needs. Its output is much smaller than that of the symbiotic nodule bacteria.
117031.m: Azotobacter fixes nitrogen even without a host plant.

117032.q: Why do many cyanobacteria keep photosynthesis separate from nitrogen fixation?
a: The enzyme nitrogenase is inhibited by oxygen
They have too little water for both
117032.e: Photosynthesis produces oxygen, which damages nitrogenase. Many filamentous cyanobacteria therefore fix nitrogen in special cells that make no oxygen, the heterocysts.

117033.q: Why do plants have to supply their nodule bacteria with a lot of sugar?
a: Nitrogen fixation needs a great deal of energy
Sugar is a building block of ammonia
Sugar protects the bacteria from frost
Without sugar the bacteria cannot breathe
117033.e: Breaking the stable triple bond in N2 costs a great deal of ATP, about 16 molecules per N2. The bacteria get this ATP from the plant's sugar.
117033.m: Biological nitrogen fixation costs a lot of energy.

117034.q: Which natural, non-biological process also fixes atmospheric nitrogen?
117034.e: The high energy of lightning makes nitrogen and oxygen react to form nitrogen oxides. These reach the soil with the rain as nitrate.
117034.m: Lightning also fixes nitrogen from the air.

117035.q: Which tree lives in symbiosis with Frankia bacteria and can therefore use atmospheric nitrogen?
117035.e: Alders form root nodules with Frankia bacteria, which resemble actinomycetes. That is why green alder in the Alps can grow even on nutrient-poor slopes.
117035.m: Alders use atmospheric nitrogen with the help of Frankia.

117036.q: Which water fern is used as green manure in Asian rice fields because of its nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria?
117036.e: The mosquito fern Azolla houses cyanobacteria of the genus Anabaena in its leaves. It has been used for centuries in rice fields as a natural nitrogen fertiliser.
117036.m: The water fern Azolla fertilises rice fields with nitrogen.

117037.q: Where do rhizobia live in symbiosis with their host plant?
a: In the wood of the trunk
117037.e: Rhizobia enter through root hairs and trigger the formation of root nodules. There they fix atmospheric nitrogen for the plant.

117038.q: Which species of rhizobia forms nodules on peas, broad beans and clover?
117038.e: Rhizobium leguminosarum occurs in different varieties, each specialised in certain host plants. Its species name refers to the legumes.
117038.m: Rhizobium leguminosarum colonises peas, beans and clover.

117039.q: What do the rhizobia receive from the plant in the symbiosis?
117039.e: The plant supplies the bacteria with products of photosynthesis as a source of energy. In return, the bacteria supply fixed nitrogen.
117039.m: The plant pays the rhizobia with sugar.

117040.q: How do rhizobia and legumes find each other in the soil?
a: The roots catch the bacteria with hairs, without any signal
Earthworms carry the bacteria to the root on purpose
117040.e: The plant releases flavonoids and so attracts the bacteria. These respond with their own signalling substances, which start nodule formation.
117040.m: Plant and rhizobia communicate with signalling substances.

117041.q: Which gas from the air can rhizobia fix in the root nodules?
117041.e: Rhizobia convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonium, which the plant can use. That is why legumes hardly need any nitrogen fertiliser.
117041.m: Rhizobia fix nitrogen from the air.

117042.q: When you cut open a root nodule, how can you tell that it is actively fixing nitrogen?
117042.e: Active nodules are pink to red inside because they contain the pigment leghaemoglobin. White or green nodules are hardly working or have stopped.
117042.m: Active nodules are pinkish red inside.

117043.q: Why are soya seeds in Switzerland often inoculated with bacteria before sowing?
a: Because the right nodule bacteria are usually missing in local soils
Because soya will not germinate otherwise
Because the bacteria keep slugs away
Because the law requires it for all seeds
117043.e: Soya comes from East Asia and needs special bradyrhizobia, which are rare in European soils. Without inoculation it forms hardly any nodules and then needs nitrogen fertiliser.
117043.m: In Switzerland, soya needs inoculated nodule bacteria.

117044.q: Why is clover-grass or peas often grown before wheat in a crop rotation?
a: Because they leave nitrogen in the soil for the next crop
Because they remove all the potassium from the soil
Because they make the soil acidic
Because they poison weeds with nitrate
117044.e: The crop and root residues of legumes contain a lot of fixed nitrogen. The following crop can use this, which saves fertiliser.
117044.m: Legumes leave nitrogen for the next crop.

117045.q: What is the chemical formula of the nitrate ion?
117045.e: Nitrate consists of one nitrogen atom and three oxygen atoms and has a single negative charge. NO2- is nitrite, NH4+ is ammonium.
117045.m: The nitrate ion has the formula NO3-.

117046.q: Which natural nitrate fertiliser was exported in large quantities from the Atacama Desert in the 19th century?
117046.e: Chile saltpetre consists mainly of sodium nitrate and was mined in northern Chile. Only the industrial synthesis of ammonia made Europe independent of it.
117046.m: Chile saltpetre was an important natural nitrate fertiliser.

117047.q: Why is nitrate easily washed into the groundwater?
a: Because it is negatively charged and hardly sticks to soil particles
Because it is heavier than water
Because it is tightly bound to clay
117047.e: The exchange sites in the soil mainly bind positively charged ions. The anion nitrate stays dissolved and moves down with the water seeping through the soil.
117047.m: Nitrate is easily washed out because the soil hardly holds on to it.

117048.q: Which powerful greenhouse gas can escape from the soil when microbes convert nitrogen fertiliser?
117048.e: Nitrous oxide is a by-product of bacterial conversion of ammonium and nitrate. It is many times more powerful than CO2 and is an important source of greenhouse gas from farming.
117048.m: The greenhouse gas nitrous oxide can escape from fertilised soils.

117049.q: What is the maximum level of nitrate allowed in drinking water in Switzerland (as of 2025)?
117049.e: The Swiss Drinking Water Ordinance sets a maximum level for nitrate of 40 mg per litre. The EU allows 50 mg per litre.
117049.m: In Switzerland, drinking water may contain at most 40 mg of nitrate per litre.

117050.q: Why is a lot of nitrate in drinking water a particular problem for babies?
a: Because it can turn into nitrite, which disturbs oxygen transport in the blood
Because nitrate turns into alcohol in the stomach
117050.e: In the body, nitrate can be reduced to nitrite. Nitrite changes the blood pigment so that it carries less oxygen; babies are particularly sensitive to this.
117050.m: Nitrite from nitrate can disturb oxygen transport in the blood.

117051.q: Which plant enzyme reduces nitrate that has been taken up to nitrite in the first step?
117051.e: Nitrate reductase converts nitrate into nitrite; ammonium is then formed via nitrite reductase. Only as ammonium is the nitrogen built into amino acids.
117051.m: Nitrate reductase turns nitrate into nitrite.

117052.q: Why does lettuce from a winter greenhouse often contain more nitrate than summer lettuce?
a: Because in low light, less nitrate is converted into protein
Because there is more nitrate in the rain in winter
Because cold attracts nitrate from the air
Because winter lettuce is not fertilised
117052.e: Converting nitrate needs energy from photosynthesis. When light is short, more unprocessed nitrate therefore builds up in the leaves.
117052.m: Low light leads to more nitrate in leafy vegetables.

117053.q: What is meant by chlorosis in plants?
a: Yellowing of the leaves due to lack of chlorophyll
Poisoning by chlorine in the watering water
A fungal disease of the roots
117053.e: In chlorosis, the plant makes too little chlorophyll or breaks it down. The leaves become pale green to yellow.
117053.m: Chlorosis is yellowing caused by a lack of chlorophyll.

117054.q: Young leaves turn yellow between veins that stay green. Which deficiency is typical of this?
117054.e: Iron hardly moves within the plant, so the deficiency shows on the youngest leaves. The green network of veins on a yellow leaf is typical.
117054.m: Iron deficiency shows as yellowing of young leaves with green veins.

117055.q: Why does iron deficiency chlorosis often occur on chalky soils, even though there is enough iron?
a: Because iron dissolves poorly at high pH
Because lime makes the iron evaporate
Because chalky soils reflect too little light
117055.e: At high pH, iron forms compounds that hardly dissolve and that roots can barely take up. This is called lime-induced chlorosis.
117055.m: On chalky soils, iron is hard for plants to get.

117056.q: Older leaves show yellow areas between green veins, while young leaves are healthy. Which deficiency is likely?
117056.e: Magnesium moves within the plant and, when it is short, is moved from old leaves into young ones. That is why the older leaves turn yellow between the veins first.
117056.m: Magnesium deficiency shows first on older leaves.

117057.q: A plant shows even yellowing that starts on the oldest leaves. Which deficiency is most likely?
117057.e: When nitrogen is short, it is taken from older leaves and moved into young shoots. The old leaves then turn yellow all over, including the veins.
117057.m: Nitrogen deficiency makes old leaves turn evenly yellow.

117058.q: What helps against chlorosis in rhododendrons on chalky soil?
a: Improving the soil with an acidic substrate such as ericaceous compost
117058.e: An acidic soil makes iron soluble again, so the roots can take it up. Lime and hard water make chlorosis worse.
117058.m: Acidic soil helps rhododendrons against chlorosis.

117059.q: Which garden plant gets chlorosis particularly easily on chalky soil?
117059.e: Rhododendrons are acid-loving plants and need acidic soil. On lime they cannot take up iron well and turn yellow.

117060.q: From which Greek word does the term chlorosis come?
117060.e: The Greek chlōros means yellowish green or pale. The same word is found in chlorophyll and chlorine.
117060.m: Chlorosis comes from the Greek word for yellowish green.

117061.q: Which of Fritz Haber's activities in the First World War still damages his reputation today?
a: He led the development and use of poison gas
He built aircraft for the air force
117061.e: Haber organised the first large chlorine gas attack at Ypres in 1915. That is why awarding him the Nobel Prize in Chemistry was controversial.
117061.m: Fritz Haber was also involved in developing poison gas.

117062.q: Under which conditions does the Haber-Bosch process typically run?
a: At several hundred °C and about 100 to 300 bar
117062.e: The classic process worked at about 500 °C and 200 bar; modern plants run somewhat lower depending on their design. High pressure shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia, and the high temperature gives a usable reaction rate.
117062.m: Haber-Bosch needs high pressure and high temperature.

117063.q: In which year did BASF in Oppau start up the first large-scale ammonia plant using the Haber-Bosch process?
117063.e: Fritz Haber achieved the synthesis in the laboratory in 1909, and Carl Bosch scaled it up to industrial size. In 1913 the first plant went into operation in Oppau near Ludwigshafen.
117063.m: The first Haber-Bosch plant started up in 1913.

117064.q: Why does high pressure favour the formation of ammonia from N2 and H2?
a: Because there are fewer gas particles on the product side
Because ammonia turns to ice under pressure
Because the catalyst only melts under pressure
117064.e: There are twice as many gas molecules on the side of the starting materials as on the product side. According to Le Chatelier's principle, high pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer particles.
117064.m: High pressure favours the side with fewer gas particles.

117065.q: How many molecules of hydrogen are needed to form 2 molecules of ammonia?
117065.e: The equation is N2 + 3 H2 gives 2 NH3. Two NH3 contain 6 hydrogen atoms, so 3 H2 molecules.
117065.m: Two ammonia molecules need three hydrogen molecules.

117066.q: Roughly what proportion of the world's energy consumption is due to ammonia synthesis?
117066.e: Ammonia synthesis is one of the most energy-intensive processes in chemistry. Estimates put it at about 1 to 2 per cent of world energy consumption.
117066.m: Ammonia synthesis uses about 1 to 2 per cent of the world's energy.

117067.q: How important is the Haber-Bosch process for feeding the world?
a: About half of humanity is fed with the help of nitrogen from artificial fertiliser
It mainly supplies protein for animal feed from the air
It has no effect on yields
117067.e: According to common estimates, only about half as many people could be fed without synthetic nitrogen fertiliser. A large part of the nitrogen in our bodies therefore comes from ammonia synthesis.
117067.m: Artificial fertiliser from Haber-Bosch feeds about half of humanity.

117068.q: Which country has the largest known reserves of phosphate rock?
117068.e: By far the largest part of the world's phosphate rock reserves lies in Morocco, including Western Sahara. Switzerland has to import all its mineral phosphorus.
117068.m: Morocco has the largest phosphate reserves in the world.

a: By treating phosphate rock with sulphuric acid
117069.e: Phosphate rock (apatite) dissolves poorly. Treated with sulphuric acid, it forms water-soluble calcium dihydrogen phosphate, which plants can take up well.
117069.m: Superphosphate is made by treating rock with sulphuric acid.

117070.q: What does the plant mainly need phosphorus for?
a: For energy transfer with ATP and for nucleic acids
As the central atom of chlorophyll
As a building block of cellulose
117070.e: Phosphorus is found in ATP, DNA, RNA and the phospholipids of membranes. Without phosphorus, energy metabolism and cell division do not work.
117070.m: Plants need phosphorus for ATP and genetic material.

117071.q: Why does phosphate hardly move in the soil?
a: Because it is bound to calcium, iron and aluminium compounds
Because it only occurs in the air
117071.e: Depending on the pH, phosphate forms poorly soluble compounds with calcium or with iron and aluminium. That is why it usually stays where it was applied.
117071.m: Phosphate is held tightly in the soil.

117072.q: Which partnership helps many plants take up phosphate that is hard to reach?
117072.e: The fine fungal threads of mycorrhiza reach a much larger volume of soil than the roots. They supply the plant with phosphate and get sugar in return.
117072.m: Mycorrhizal fungi help with phosphate uptake.

117073.q: What does the Swiss Waste Ordinance (VVEA) require for sewage sludge from 2026?
a: It must be spread on fields
It may be exported to the sea
117073.e: Sewage sludge and meat-and-bone meal contain a lot of phosphorus. The Waste Ordinance requires this to be recovered from 2026, to reduce dependence on imports.
117073.m: From 2026, Switzerland requires phosphorus to be recovered from sewage sludge.

117074.q: Which toxic heavy metal is often present as an impurity in mineral phosphate fertilisers?
117074.e: Many phosphate rocks naturally contain cadmium, and some also uranium. These pollutants can build up in the soil after many years of fertilising.

117075.q: Which natural fertiliser made from seabird droppings was an important source of phosphate and nitrogen in the 19th century?
117075.e: Guano lay in thick layers on islands off Peru and was shipped to Europe in large quantities. Later, mineral fertilisers replaced the exhausted deposits.
117075.m: Guano is fertiliser made from bird droppings.

117076.q: Why do carnivorous plants catch animals?
a: To get nitrogen and phosphorus on nutrient-poor soils
Because they do not carry out photosynthesis
To protect themselves from being eaten
117076.e: Carnivorous plants often grow in bogs and on acidic, poor soils. Their prey supplies them mainly with nitrogen and phosphorus.
117076.m: Carnivorous plants top up their nutrients with prey.

117077.q: Where do carnivorous plants mainly get their energy from?
a: From the sugar in their prey
From the warmth of the soil
117077.e: Carnivorous plants are green and make their own sugar through photosynthesis. Their prey serves mainly as a source of nutrients, not of energy.
117077.m: Carnivorous plants also live on photosynthesis.

117078.q: Which animal on Borneo uses the pitchers of the pitcher plant Nepenthes lowii as a toilet and so supplies it with nutrients?
117078.e: Mountain treeshrews lick sweet sap from the pitcher lid and leave droppings in the pitcher while doing so. These droppings supply the plant with a large part of its nitrogen.
117078.m: Some pitcher plants live on treeshrew droppings.

117079.q: Where does the Venus flytrap occur naturally?
a: In North and South Carolina in the USA
117079.e: The Venus flytrap grows wild only in a small area on the coast of North and South Carolina. There it grows on damp, nutrient-poor sandy ground.
117079.m: The Venus flytrap comes from the Carolinas in the USA.

117080.q: Which carnivorous plant grows in Swiss raised bogs and catches insects with sticky glandular hairs?
117080.e: The round-leaved sundew has red glandular tentacles with shiny sticky drops. It is native to Swiss raised bogs and is protected.
117080.m: The sundew is a sticky trap from Swiss bogs.

117081.q: What type of trap does the bladderwort (Utricularia) have?
117081.e: The small bladders of the bladderwort are under negative pressure. When a small animal touches the trapdoor, it is sucked in within a fraction of a second.
117081.m: The bladderwort catches prey with suction traps.

117082.q: Which carnivorous plant with greasy, shiny leaf rosettes grows in damp Alpine meadows?
117082.e: The leaves of the butterwort (Pinguicula) are covered with sticky glands on which small insects get stuck. Several species occur in Switzerland, such as the Alpine butterwort.
117082.m: The butterwort catches insects on sticky leaves.

117083.q: How do pitcher plants (Nepenthes) catch their prey?
a: With pitfall traps that insects slide into
With leaf halves that snap shut
117083.e: The pitchers have a slippery rim and digestive fluid at the bottom. Insects that are lured in slip off and are slowly digested.
117083.m: Pitcher plants catch prey in pitfall traps.

117084.q: Which naturalist published the book “Insectivorous Plants” about carnivorous plants in 1875?
117084.e: Charles Darwin studied the sundew and other species in many experiments. His book was the first to prove that these plants really digest their prey.
117084.m: Darwin was one of the first to study carnivorous plants.

a: Plants grow without soil in a nutrient solution
Plants grow only under water in an aquarium
Plants are only watered with rainwater
117085.e: In hydroponics, plants root in water or a nutrient-free substrate. They get all their nutrients from a dissolved nutrient solution.
117085.m: Hydroponics means growing plants without soil.

117086.q: Which substrate is used particularly often for indoor hydroponics?
117086.e: Expanded clay consists of fired, porous clay balls. It gives the plant support, stores some water and lets air reach the roots.
117086.m: Expanded clay is the typical hydroponic substrate.

117087.q: What is the water level indicator on a hydroponic plant for?
a: It shows when nutrient solution needs topping up
It measures the temperature of the roots
It shows the nitrate content of the leaves
117087.e: The float in the indicator sinks with the liquid level. When it shows minimum, you top up, but not above optimum, so that the roots get air.
117087.m: The water level indicator shows when to top up.

117088.q: What is the nutrient film technique (NFT) in hydroponics?
a: A thin film of nutrient solution flows constantly past the roots in channels
The roots are wrapped in plastic film
The leaves are sprayed with a nutrient film
The plants stand in solid gelatine
117088.e: In the nutrient film technique, the plants stand in slightly sloping channels. The nutrient solution flows through as a thin film, so the roots get nutrients and air at the same time.
117088.m: In NFT, a thin film of nutrient solution flows past the roots.

117089.q: How are the roots supplied with nutrients in aeroponics?
a: They hang in the air and are sprayed with nutrient solution
They sit in sand with slow-release fertiliser
They stand permanently in tap water
117089.e: In aeroponics, the roots hang freely in a chamber and are regularly sprayed with a fine mist. This gives them a particularly large amount of oxygen.
117089.m: In aeroponics, freely hanging roots are sprayed.

117090.q: What does the EC value of a nutrient solution measure?
a: The electrical conductivity as a measure of dissolved nutrient salts
How much light it lets through
117090.e: Dissolved salts conduct electricity, so conductivity rises with nutrient concentration. The EC value therefore shows how strongly the solution is fertilised.
117090.m: The EC value shows the salt concentration of the nutrient solution.

117091.q: In which pH range is a nutrient solution kept for most hydroponic plants?
117091.e: In this slightly acidic range, most nutrients, especially iron and phosphate, are readily available. At higher values some nutrients come out of solution.
117091.m: Nutrient solutions should be slightly acidic.

117092.q: What did researchers prove in the 19th century when they grew plants in water with precisely known salts?
a: Plants need certain minerals, but not soil
117092.e: Around 1860, Julius Sachs and Wilhelm Knop grew plants in nutrient solutions. In this way they showed which minerals plants really need and that soil is not necessary for this.
117092.m: Plants need minerals, not necessarily soil.

117093.q: What does the cation exchange capacity (CEC) of a soil describe?
a: How many cations it can bind in exchangeable form
How quickly it lets water drain away
How much it warms up in the sun
117093.e: The CEC shows how many positively charged ions the soil can hold on its surfaces and release again. It is a measure of its ability to store nutrients.
117093.m: The CEC measures how many cations a soil can store.

117094.q: Why is a soil with a high cation exchange capacity usually more fertile?
a: It holds on to nutrients such as potassium and calcium
It lets water drain away faster
117094.e: A high CEC means many sites to which positively charged nutrients stick. So they are not washed out and remain available to plants.
117094.m: A high CEC holds nutrients in the soil.

117095.q: Which soil components contribute most to the cation exchange capacity?
117095.e: Humus and clay minerals have very large, negatively charged surfaces. Sand and gravel, on the other hand, consist mainly of quartz with a small surface area.
117095.m: Humus and clay store the most nutrients.

117096.q: Why can clay particles hold on to cations?
a: Because their surfaces are mostly negatively charged
117096.e: Clay minerals carry surplus negative charges because of ion substitution in their crystal lattice. Positively charged ions such as Ca2+, Mg2+ or K+ attach to these.
117096.m: Negative charges on clay particles hold on to cations.

117097.q: What is a consequence of the low cation exchange capacity of a sandy soil?
a: The soil stores a particularly large amount of potassium
117097.e: Sandy soils can hold on to only a few cations. Fertiliser should therefore be spread in small doses so that it is not lost with the water seeping through.

117098.q: What happens when acid rain fills more and more of a soil's exchange sites with hydrogen ions?
a: Nutrients such as calcium are pushed out and washed away
117098.e: Hydrogen ions push calcium, magnesium and potassium off the exchange sites. These nutrients are lost with the water seeping through, and the soil becomes even more acidic.
117098.m: Acidic soils lose nutrients to the water seeping through.

117099.q: Why do some clay soils swell up a lot in rain and crack in drought?
a: Their clay minerals take in water between their layers
They contain a particularly large amount of lime
They consist mainly of sand grains
Earthworms loosen them when it rains
117099.e: Swelling clay minerals such as montmorillonite take in water between their layers. Their large internal surface also gives them a high cation exchange capacity.
117099.m: Swelling clay minerals take in water between their layers.

117100.q: Why are acidic arable soils limed?
a: So that the soil can store nutrients better
So that the soil dries out faster
So that the soil contains more sand
So that earthworms are driven away
117100.e: Lime raises the pH. In less acidic soil, more exchange sites on humus and clay are free for nutrients such as calcium, magnesium and potassium.
117100.m: Liming improves nutrient storage in acidic soils.

117200.q: In which blood vessels is blood pressure highest?
a: In the large arteries close to the heart
In the veins of the feet
117200.e: The left ventricle pumps blood at high pressure into the aorta and the large arteries. On its way through the vessels the pressure keeps falling.
117200.m: Blood pressure is highest in the arteries close to the heart.

117201.q: What does the systolic blood pressure value refer to?
a: The highest pressure while the heart is pumping out blood
The lowest pressure in the filling phase
The pressure in the pulmonary veins
The pressure in the right atrium
117201.e: The systolic value is the peak pressure in the arteries when the left ventricle pumps out blood. The diastolic value is the lowest pressure in the relaxation phase.
117201.m: The systolic value is the upper blood pressure value.

117203.q: When measuring blood pressure by hand, what do you hear with the stethoscope in the crook of the elbow?
a: Sounds of blood flowing in the artery
117203.e: When the cuff pressure is slowly released, blood spurts through the squeezed artery. These sounds show the upper and lower blood pressure values.
117203.m: When measuring blood pressure, you hear blood flowing through the artery.

117204.q: According to the “Ohm's law” of the circulation, which two quantities determine mean blood pressure?
117204.e: Blood pressure roughly equals cardiac output times total peripheral resistance. If one of them rises, the pressure rises too.
117204.m: Blood pressure comes from cardiac output times vessel resistance.

117205.q: Mean arterial pressure is roughly the diastolic value plus one third of the difference to the systolic value. What is it at 120/80 mmHg?
117205.e: 80 + (120 minus 80) / 3 gives about 93 mmHg. The mean pressure is closer to the lower value because the heart spends longer relaxing than contracting.
117205.m: Mean pressure is closer to the diastolic than to the systolic value.

117206.q: The flow resistance of a vessel depends on the fourth power of the radius. By what factor does it rise if the radius is halved?
117206.e: Resistance is inversely proportional to r to the power of 4. If the radius is halved, resistance rises by 2 to the power of 4, that is 16 times.
117206.m: Even small narrowings of a vessel raise resistance a lot.

117207.q: Which hormone from the adrenal medulla makes blood pressure and pulse rise quickly under stress?
117207.e: Under stress the adrenal medulla releases adrenaline. It speeds up the heartbeat and narrows many blood vessels, so blood pressure rises.
117207.m: Adrenaline drives up blood pressure and pulse.

117208.q: Which organ is most important for regulating blood pressure in the long term?
117208.e: The kidney controls blood volume through the excretion of salt and water. In this way it determines blood pressure over days and weeks.
117208.m: The kidney regulates blood pressure in the long run.

117209.q: Which stimulus do baroreceptors in the vessel wall react to?
117209.e: Baroreceptors are stretch receptors. If blood pressure rises, the vessel wall is stretched more and they fire more often.
117209.m: Baroreceptors measure blood pressure through the stretching of the wall.

117210.q: Where are the most important pressure sensors (baroreceptors) for arterial blood pressure?
a: In the carotid artery and the aortic arch
In the veins of the legs
In the alveoli of the lungs
117210.e: The most important arterial baroreceptors sit at the fork of the carotid artery and in the aortic arch, so close to the heart and on the way to the brain.
117210.m: The carotid artery and aortic arch contain the most important pressure sensors.

117211.q: In which part of the brain is the cardiovascular centre that processes the signals from the baroreceptors?
117211.e: The cardiovascular centre lies in the medulla oblongata. There the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems are adjusted.
117211.m: The cardiovascular centre sits in the medulla oblongata.

117212.q: What does the baroreceptor reflex do when blood pressure suddenly rises?
117212.e: More stretch leads to more signals to the cardiovascular centre. It damps down the sympathetic system and activates the vagus, so heart rate and pressure fall.
117212.m: When pressure is high, the baroreceptor reflex slows the heart.

117213.q: By which route do the baroreceptors' signals reach the cardiovascular centre?
a: Through hormones in the blood to the kidney
Through the spinal cord to the cerebellum
Through the lymph to the spleen
117213.e: The baroreceptors send their signals through cranial nerves such as the vagus to the cardiovascular centre in the brainstem. This lets the body react within seconds.
117213.m: Baroreceptors report the pressure to the brainstem through nerves.

117214.q: Why can strong pressure on the side of the carotid artery slow the heart?
a: The pressure sensors wrongly report high blood pressure
The carotid artery is completely blocked
The heart gets too little oxygen
The larynx presses on the heart
117214.e: Pressure from outside stretches the wall of the carotid artery. The brain interprets this as a rise in blood pressure and slows the heart by reflex.
117214.m: Pressure on the carotid artery can slow the heart.

117215.q: Which kind of blood pressure regulation is the baroreceptor reflex mainly responsible for?
117215.e: The reflex evens out short-term fluctuations, for example when standing up. With permanently high pressure the receptors adjust to a higher level.
117215.m: The baroreceptor reflex acts quickly, but only in the short term.

117216.q: What happens to the baroreceptors when blood pressure is permanently raised?
117216.e: In chronic hypertension the set point of the baroreceptors shifts upwards. The high pressure is then no longer reported as a deviation.
117216.m: Baroreceptors get used to permanently high pressure.

117217.q: In which organ is the enzyme renin made?
117217.e: Renin is made by specialised cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus in the kidney. They sit on the arterioles leading into the glomeruli.

117218.q: Which stimulus mainly leads to the release of renin?
a: Falling blood pressure in the kidney
117218.e: If the pressure in the kidney vessels or the amount of salt at the macula densa falls, more renin is released. The sympathetic system also stimulates the release.
117218.m: Low pressure in the kidney triggers renin release.

117219.q: Which protein does renin split into angiotensin I?
117219.e: Renin splits angiotensinogen, which is made in the liver. This produces angiotensin I, which has hardly any effect yet.
117219.m: Renin cuts angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.

117220.q: Which enzyme converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II?
117220.e: ACE, mainly on the lining of the lung vessels, turns angiotensin I into the highly effective angiotensin II.
117220.m: ACE produces the active angiotensin II.

117221.e: Aldosterone is made in the outermost layer of the adrenal cortex, the zona glomerulosa. Angiotensin II stimulates its production.
117221.m: Aldosterone comes from the adrenal cortex.

117222.q: What does aldosterone do in the kidney tubules?
117222.e: In the collecting duct, aldosterone promotes the reabsorption of sodium and the excretion of potassium. Water follows the sodium, and blood volume rises.
117222.m: Aldosterone keeps sodium, and with it water, in the body.

117223.q: Which side effect is typical of ACE inhibitors?
a: A green discolouration of the skin
Loss of the sense of smell
117223.e: ACE also breaks down bradykinin. If it is inhibited, bradykinin builds up, which often triggers a dry cough.
117223.m: ACE inhibitors often cause an irritating cough.

117224.q: How do blood pressure medicines of the sartan group work?
a: They block the angiotensin II receptor
They inhibit renin production in the liver
117224.e: Sartans such as losartan occupy the AT1 receptor. Angiotensin II can then no longer narrow the vessels.
117224.m: Sartans protect the vessels from angiotensin II.

117225.q: From which natural model was the first ACE inhibitor, captopril, developed?
a: From the venom of a lancehead viper
117225.e: Peptides that inhibit ACE were found in the venom of the Brazilian snake Bothrops jararaca. They served as the model for captopril.
117225.m: A snake venom led to ACE inhibitors.

117226.q: From which values measured at the doctor's surgery does the usual European definition speak of high blood pressure?
117226.e: According to European guidelines, a value of 140/90 mmHg or more measured repeatedly at the surgery counts as hypertension. Values below that can still be raised.
117226.m: From 140/90 mmHg it is called high blood pressure.

117227.q: Why is high blood pressure often called a “silent killer”?
a: It causes no symptoms for a long time
117227.e: Many people affected feel nothing for years while their vessels, heart and kidneys are already being damaged. That is why regular measurements are important.
117227.m: High blood pressure often does harm without causing pain.

117228.q: What is the most common form of high blood pressure without a single identifiable cause called?
117228.e: In about nine out of ten people affected, no single cause is found. This is called primary or essential hypertension.
117228.m: Most high blood pressure has no single cause.

117229.q: Which organ can cause secondary hypertension if it makes too much aldosterone?
117229.e: The adrenal cortex makes the hormone aldosterone. If there is too much of it, the body holds back sodium and water and blood pressure rises.
117229.m: Too much aldosterone from the adrenal gland raises blood pressure.

117230.q: How does the left ventricle react to years of raised blood pressure?
a: It shrinks to the size of an atrium
117230.e: The heart constantly has to pump against higher pressure. The muscle grows as with training, causing left ventricular hypertrophy.
117230.m: High blood pressure thickens the wall of the left ventricle.

117231.q: Which dietary measure has been shown to lower blood pressure in many people?
117231.e: A lot of sodium binds water in the body and so increases blood volume. A diet lower in salt lowers blood pressure in many people affected.
117231.m: Less salt often helps against high blood pressure.

117232.q: What is 24-hour blood pressure monitoring for?
a: It shows the pattern over day and night
It measures the pressure in the lungs
117232.e: A portable device takes measurements at intervals all day and during the night. This reveals, for example, white coat hypertension or a missing fall in pressure at night.
117232.m: Long-term monitoring shows blood pressure in everyday life.

a: Very high blood pressure with acute organ damage
Slightly raised blood pressure without symptoms
A sudden drop in blood pressure
A high pulse with normal blood pressure
117233.e: In a hypertensive emergency, blood pressure is greatly raised and acutely damages organs such as the brain, heart or kidneys. It must be treated in hospital immediately.
117233.m: A hypertensive emergency needs immediate treatment.

117234.q: Which organ can be so damaged by years of high blood pressure that dialysis becomes necessary?
117234.e: High pressure damages the fine vessels of the renal corpuscles. In the long term kidney function can fall so much that blood cleaning by dialysis is needed.
117234.m: High blood pressure can destroy the kidneys.

117235.q: From which values do doctors usually speak of low blood pressure in adults?
117235.e: Values below about 100/60 mmHg usually count as hypotension. However, many people with such values have no symptoms.
117235.m: Low blood pressure is below about 100/60 mmHg.

117236.q: What is a drop in blood pressure that occurs when standing up quickly called?
117236.e: When you stand up, blood sinks into the legs. If the circulation reacts too slowly, the pressure falls and you feel dizzy.
117236.m: Dizziness on standing up comes from a drop in blood pressure.

117237.q: How does a doctor check whether the circulation reacts well when standing up?
a: Blood pressure and pulse are measured lying down and then standing
Temperature is measured before and after eating
The person is made to run for ten minutes
Blood sugar is measured while sitting
117237.e: In the so-called Schellong test, blood pressure and pulse lying down and standing are compared. If blood pressure drops sharply, there is an orthostatic disorder.
117237.m: A lying-standing test checks the circulation's reaction to standing up.

117238.q: What is a brief loss of consciousness due to a temporary lack of blood flow to the brain called?
117238.e: In a syncope, blood pressure briefly falls so much that the brain gets too little blood. Lying down, people usually recover quickly.
117238.m: The medical term for fainting is syncope.

117239.q: What helps many people with low blood pressure in everyday life?
a: Drinking enough and standing up slowly
Taking hot baths for as long as possible
Drinking little and standing up quickly
117239.e: Enough fluid increases blood volume. Standing up slowly gives the circulation time to adjust.
117239.m: Drinking and standing up slowly help with low blood pressure.

117240.q: Why can compression stockings help with low blood pressure?
a: They stop blood from pooling in the leg veins
117240.e: Pressure from outside reduces the diameter of the leg veins. This lets more blood flow back to the heart and keeps the pressure more stable.
117240.m: Compression stockings stop blood from staying in the legs.

117241.q: Which life-threatening condition with a sharp drop in blood pressure can develop after heavy blood loss?
117241.e: If a lot of blood volume is missing, the heart cannot pump out enough. Blood pressure falls and organs are no longer adequately supplied.
117241.m: Heavy blood loss can trigger shock.

117242.q: How does the body normally react to a drop in blood pressure on standing up?
a: The pulse rises and vessels narrow
The pulse falls and vessels widen
117242.e: Less stretching of the baroreceptors activates the sympathetic system. Heart rate and vessel tension increase, and blood pressure is maintained.
117242.m: When you stand up, the body speeds up the heart.

a: A blocked blood vessel in the brain
117244.e: About four out of five strokes are ischaemic. A blood clot blocks an artery in the brain, and the tissue beyond it no longer gets oxygen.
117244.m: A clot usually causes the stroke.

117245.q: In the FAST test, what does the letter T stand for?
a: The time until you call the emergency number
117245.e: FAST stands for Face, Arms, Speech and Time. The T reminds you to call the emergency number immediately, because every minute counts.
117245.m: With a stroke, every minute counts.

117246.q: What is a stroke called that is caused by a blood vessel in the brain bursting?
117246.e: In a haemorrhagic stroke, blood leaks into the brain tissue. The most common cause is blood pressure that has been too high for a long time.
117246.m: A brain haemorrhage is a haemorrhagic stroke.

117247.q: Which treatment dissolves the blood clot with medicines in an ischaemic stroke?
117247.e: In thrombolysis a substance that dissolves the clot is injected. It is only possible within a narrow time window after the symptoms begin.
117247.m: Thrombolysis dissolves clots in the brain.

117248.q: Up to how many hours after symptoms begin is thrombolysis usually possible for a stroke?
117248.e: Thrombolysis is usually used up to about 4.5 hours after symptoms begin. After that the risks of bleeding outweigh the benefits.
117248.m: There is only a little time for thrombolysis in a stroke.

117249.q: What is done in a mechanical thrombectomy?
a: The clot is pulled out with a catheter
Part of the skull is replaced
117249.e: Through a catheter from the groin, the clot is removed from the artery in the brain. The method is suitable for blockages of large vessels.
117249.m: In a thrombectomy the clot is taken out.

117250.q: Which heart rhythm disorder is a common cause of blood clots that trigger a stroke?
117250.e: In atrial fibrillation the atrium no longer contracts properly. Clots form in the still blood and can be washed into the brain.
117250.m: Atrial fibrillation increases the risk of stroke.

117251.q: What is a transient ischaemic attack?
a: Brief stroke symptoms that disappear quickly
117251.e: In a TIA, signs of a stroke appear that usually go away within minutes. It is considered an urgent warning sign of a coming stroke.
117251.m: A TIA is a serious warning signal.

117252.q: Where does the blood clot in a pulmonary embolism usually come from?
a: From a deep vein in the leg
117252.e: Usually a clot breaks free from a deep vein thrombosis in the leg or pelvis. It reaches the pulmonary arteries through the right side of the heart.
117252.m: Pulmonary embolisms usually begin in the leg veins.

117253.q: Through which ventricle of the heart does a clot from the leg veins reach the lungs?
117253.e: Venous blood flows through the vena cava into the right atrium and right ventricle. From there it is pumped into the pulmonary artery.
117253.m: A venous clot passes through the right side of the heart.

117254.q: Which set of symptoms is typical of a pulmonary embolism?
117254.e: Typical signs are sudden breathlessness, pain when breathing and a fast pulse. Large embolisms can lead to circulatory failure.
117254.m: Sudden breathlessness can point to a pulmonary embolism.

117255.q: Which factor encourages a thrombosis to form?
a: Good blood flow to the skin
117255.e: Rudolf Virchow named three causes: damage to the vessel wall, slowed blood flow and increased clotting of the blood. This is called Virchow's triad.

117256.q: Which blood test helps rule out a pulmonary embolism when suspicion is low?
117256.e: D-dimers are breakdown products of fibrin. If the value is normal and the probability is low, a pulmonary embolism is very unlikely.
117256.m: Normal D-dimers speak against a fresh thrombosis.

117257.q: Which imaging method is usually used today to detect a pulmonary embolism?
117257.e: In CT angiography contrast medium is injected. Clots in the pulmonary arteries then show up as gaps.
117257.m: CT angiography shows clots in the pulmonary arteries.

117258.q: Which group of medicines is the basis of treatment for a pulmonary embolism?
117258.e: Anticoagulants such as heparin stop the clot from growing and new ones from forming. The body can then break down the plug itself.
117258.m: Anticoagulants are the basis of embolism treatment.

117259.q: Why do long flights increase the risk of a pulmonary embolism?
a: Sitting for a long time slows blood flow in the legs
The high-altitude air thins the blood
The airline food thickens the blood
117259.e: When sitting for a long time the calf muscle pump hardly works and the veins are bent. The blood flows more slowly and clots more easily.
117259.m: On long journeys you should move your legs.

117260.q: Which group of substances does cholesterol belong to?
117260.e: Cholesterol is a sterol with the typical steroid skeleton of four rings. It belongs to the lipids.

117261.q: What job does cholesterol have in the cell membrane?
117261.e: Cholesterol slots in between the phospholipids. It makes the membrane more stable but not rigid.

117262.q: Which organ makes most of the body's own cholesterol?
117262.e: The liver is the most important place where cholesterol is made. The body makes more cholesterol itself than it takes in with food.

117263.q: What is the basic skeleton of the cholesterol molecule made of?
a: A long chain of amino acids
117263.e: Cholesterol has the typical steroid skeleton of four rings. All steroid hormones share this basic skeleton.
117263.m: Cholesterol has a skeleton of four rings.

117264.q: Which components of bile are made from cholesterol in the liver?
117264.e: The liver converts cholesterol into bile acids. In the gut these help to emulsify and absorb fats.
117264.m: The liver makes bile acids from cholesterol.

117265.q: What are medicines from the statin group used for?
a: To lower a cholesterol level that is too high
117265.e: Statins slow a key enzyme of cholesterol production in the liver. As a result LDL cholesterol in the blood falls and the risk of heart attacks decreases.

117266.q: Which stress hormone is made from cholesterol?
117266.e: Cortisol is a steroid hormone of the adrenal cortex. Like all steroid hormones, it is made from cholesterol.

117267.q: Why does cholesterol in the blood need transport particles?
a: It is hardly soluble in water
It is poisonous to blood cells
117267.e: Cholesterol is fat-soluble and does not dissolve in watery blood. It is therefore transported in lipoproteins with a coat of proteins and phospholipids.
117267.m: Cholesterol travels in the blood in lipoproteins.

117268.q: What does the abbreviation LDL stand for?
117268.e: LDL means low-density lipoprotein. Compared with its protein it contains a lot of fat and is therefore light.

117269.q: In which direction does LDL mainly transport cholesterol?
a: From the liver to the body's cells
From the body's cells to the liver
From the gut to the lungs
From the kidney to the gut
117269.e: LDL delivers cholesterol from the liver to the tissues. Too much of it can build up in vessel walls.
117269.m: LDL brings cholesterol to the cells.

117270.q: Why is LDL cholesterol often called “bad” cholesterol?
117270.e: A lot of LDL gets into the vessel wall and is altered there. It contributes to the formation of plaques and so to arteriosclerosis.
117270.m: A lot of LDL harms the arteries.

117271.q: How do cells take up LDL particles from the blood?
117271.e: The LDL receptor binds LDL on the cell surface. It is then taken in by endocytosis.
117271.m: The LDL receptor brings LDL into the cell.

117272.q: How do statins lower the LDL level in the blood?
a: They inhibit cholesterol production in the liver
They stop fat being absorbed in the stomach
117272.e: Statins slow a key enzyme of cholesterol production. The liver cells then make more LDL receptors and take more LDL out of the blood, as Brown and Goldstein showed.
117272.m: Statins lower LDL through the liver.

117273.q: Which hereditary disease with a faulty LDL receptor leads to very high LDL levels?
117273.e: In familial hypercholesterolaemia the LDL receptor works poorly. LDL stays in the blood, and heart attacks can occur early.
117273.m: A faulty LDL receptor raises LDL sharply.

117274.q: What are the eating cells in the vessel wall called that have stuffed themselves with oxidised LDL?
117274.e: Macrophages take up altered LDL and fill with fat droplets. Under the microscope they look foamy and form the core of early plaques.
117274.m: Foam cells are an early sign of arteriosclerosis.

117275.q: Roughly how is an LDL particle built?
a: A fatty core with a coat of protein and phospholipids
A red blood cell loaded with fat
117275.e: Fat does not dissolve in water. In LDL, cholesterol and fats lie inside, while phospholipids and the protein apolipoprotein B-100 sit on the outside.
117275.m: LDL is a ball of fat with a water-soluble coat.

117276.q: What does the abbreviation HDL stand for?
117276.e: HDL means high-density lipoprotein. It contains a relatively large amount of protein and little fat.

117277.q: What is the main job of HDL in fat metabolism?
a: Bringing cholesterol back to the liver
117277.e: HDL takes up excess cholesterol from tissues and vessel walls and brings it to the liver. This is called reverse cholesterol transport.
117277.m: HDL brings cholesterol back to the liver.

117278.q: Why is HDL cholesterol often called “good” cholesterol?
a: It removes cholesterol from the vessels
It supplies energy for the brain
117278.e: Because HDL carries cholesterol away from the vessel wall, higher levels are linked with less arteriosclerosis.
117278.m: HDL helps clear cholesterol from the vessels.

117279.q: Which lipoprotein is often called “bad” cholesterol?
117279.e: LDL brings cholesterol from the liver to the tissues. Too much LDL encourages deposits in the vessel walls.
117279.m: LDL counts as bad cholesterol, HDL as good cholesterol.

117280.q: Which lifestyle habit has been shown to raise HDL cholesterol?
117280.e: Endurance training raises the HDL level. Smoking and lack of exercise, on the other hand, lower it.

117281.q: What does a very low HDL level mean for cardiovascular risk?
117281.e: Low HDL levels count as a risk factor for arteriosclerosis. An important way of removing cholesterol from the vessels is missing.
117281.m: Little HDL is bad for the vessels.

117282.q: Which class of lipoprotein has the highest density?
117282.e: Density increases with the share of protein. HDL has the most protein, chylomicrons the most fat and the lowest density.
117282.m: The more protein, the denser the lipoprotein.

117283.q: What is a lipoprotein such as HDL?
a: A transport particle of protein and fat in the blood
An enzyme for digesting fat in the stomach
117283.e: Fats do not dissolve in water. That is why cholesterol and other fats are transported in the blood in particles with a coat of proteins.
117283.m: Lipoproteins transport fats in the blood.

117284.q: What job do venous valves have?
a: They stop blood from flowing backwards
They filter bacteria out of the blood
117284.e: Venous valves are pockets that only open towards the heart. If blood flows back, they close.
117284.m: Venous valves only let blood flow towards the heart.

117285.q: What is the mechanism called in which muscles squeeze the leg veins and press the blood towards the heart?
117285.e: When the leg muscles tense, they press on the deep veins. The valves make sure that the blood only flows upwards.
117285.m: When walking, the calf muscles pump blood to the heart.

117286.q: In which part of the body are there especially many venous valves?
117286.e: In the legs the blood has to flow upwards against gravity. That is why leg veins have many valves.
117286.m: The legs need especially many venous valves.

117287.q: Which condition often develops when the valves in the superficial leg veins no longer close?
117287.e: If the valves close poorly, blood backs up and the veins widen. Twisting varicose veins develop, medically called varices.
117287.m: Leaky venous valves lead to varicose veins.

117288.q: Which English doctor used the venous valves in 1628 as an argument for the circulation of the blood?
117288.e: William Harvey showed that the valves only let blood flow towards the heart. This supported his theory of a closed blood circulation.
117288.m: Harvey used the venous valves to prove the circulation.

117289.q: Which large veins have no venous valves?
117289.e: The superior and inferior vena cava have no valves. Here mainly the suction from breathing and the heart is at work.
117289.m: The venae cavae have no valves.

117290.q: What is the chronic disease with swelling and skin changes caused by damaged venous valves called?
117290.e: In chronic venous insufficiency, blood backs up in the legs. This leads to oedema, discolouration and in the worst case to a leg ulcer.
117290.m: Broken venous valves cause blood to back up in the legs.

117291.q: From which layer of the vessel wall are venous valves formed?
a: From the outer connective tissue layer
117291.e: Venous valves are folds of the intima, the innermost layer of the wall. They are covered with endothelium.
117291.m: Venous valves are folds of the vessel's inner lining.

a: A bypass route for the blood
The flow of lymph in the gut
117292.e: If a vessel is narrowed or blocked, blood can flow through side vessels. This bypass is called collateral circulation.

117293.q: Why does a blockage of one carotid artery not always lead to a stroke?
a: A ring of vessels at the base of the brain redirects blood
The neck veins take over the supply
The heart then beats twice as fast
117293.e: The circle of Willis at the base of the brain connects the carotid arteries and the vertebral arteries. If one supply fails, blood can be redirected through this ring.
117293.m: The circle of Willis secures the brain's blood supply.

117294.q: What can form when blood backs up in front of a scarred liver?
a: A hole in the septum of the heart
117294.e: In cirrhosis of the liver, blood backs up in the portal vein. It takes a detour through veins of the oesophagus, which widen into varices and can bleed heavily.
117294.m: Blood backing up in front of the liver can cause varicose veins in the oesophagus.

117295.q: Why can thick veins sometimes be seen on the belly when blood backs up badly in front of the liver?
a: The blood looks for detours past the liver
The stomach muscles push the veins outwards
The skin becomes thinner and transparent
The heart pumps too little blood into the legs
117295.e: If blood cannot flow through the liver, it takes a detour through veins in the skin of the belly. These widen in a star shape around the navel; this picture is called caput medusae.
117295.m: Widened belly veins show a bypass circulation around the liver.

117296.q: With an inborn narrowing of the aorta, the pulse in the legs is often weak. Why?
a: Less blood arrives beyond the narrowing
The leg muscles need no oxygen
117296.e: In coarctation of the aorta, the main artery is narrowed after the arm arteries branch off. The arms get plenty of blood, the legs less; bypasses through the rib arteries only partly make up for this.
117296.m: A narrowing in the aorta reduces blood flow to the legs.
